attributes.label: Hotter, drier summers
attributes.description: Summers with less rain and more evaporation. Around 2050 (2036–2065), against 1991–2020, every KNMI'23 scenario has 2 to 13% less summer rain, 6 to 11% more potential evaporation in summer and a largest precipitation deficit of April to September 13 to 35% larger, and the great rivers carry less water in summer (KNMI, 2023, pp. 3–4, 42). Measured as national averages, evaporation over five stations, Vlissingen among them (p. 5): this report gives no rain or deficit number for Zeeland, which appears only on maps of the whole country, West Europe or Europe, in colour classes, for the present and around 2100 (pp. 15, 24, 27). Set outside the island: a Constant.
attributes.sources: KNMI. (2023). KNMI’23-klimaatscenario’s voor Nederland (KNMI-Publicatie 23-03). https://www.knmi.nl/kennis-en-datacentrum/publicatie/knmi-23-klimaatscenario-s-voor-nederland

attributes.label: Sea-level rise
attributes.description: The mean level of the sea at the Dutch coast. Around 2050 (2036–2065) every KNMI'23 scenario has it 16 to 38 cm above 1995–2014, 24 cm in the low-emission scenarios and 27 cm in the high, still rising by 1 to 8 mm a year (KNMI, 2023, pp. 3, 5). Set outside the island: a Constant.
attributes.sources: KNMI. (2023). KNMI’23-klimaatscenario’s voor Nederland (KNMI-Publicatie 23-03). https://www.knmi.nl/kennis-en-datacentrum/publicatie/knmi-23-klimaatscenario-s-voor-nederland

attributes.label: Wetter winters
attributes.description: More rain in winter. Around 2050 (2036–2065), against 1991–2020, every KNMI'23 scenario has 4 to 7% more winter rain, and 0.4 to 0.8 more days a winter with 10 mm or more (KNMI, 2023, p. 3). Measured as a national average over 13 rain stations (p. 5): this report gives no number for Zeeland, which appears only on maps of Europe and West Europe around 2100, in colour classes (pp. 15, 24). Set outside the island: a Constant.
attributes.sources: KNMI. (2023). KNMI’23-klimaatscenario’s voor Nederland (KNMI-Publicatie 23-03). https://www.knmi.nl/kennis-en-datacentrum/publicatie/knmi-23-klimaatscenario-s-voor-nederland

attributes.label: Rainwater lens  recharge in the low  polders
attributes.description: The rain that soaks in and refills the rainwater lenses of the low polders: mostly the winter's rain surplus, since in summer most of the rain evaporates (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 155, for the Netherlands). On Schouwen-Duiveland upward saline seepage keeps it within the clay and peat top layer of the low polders (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3662, 3674–3675), and tile drains usually discharge shallow groundwater rapidly during rain, as other studies found (p. 3661); recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness, by measurements on the island and a model built from them (pp. 3662, 3673–3675).

Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(3), 153–163. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17866
de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011

attributes.label: Rainwater lens  thickness in the low  polders
attributes.description: The thickness of the fresh rainwater lenses on top of the saline groundwater in the island's low polders, from the surface to the middle of the mixing zone between them: about 2 m on average in the low-lying polders with saline seepage, under 2 m over more than half of the 56 km² surveyed (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island from a helicopter and on the ground). These lenses keep salt out of the root zone and reach only the crop on their own field. A Stock: a year's recharge barely moves it (Rainwater lens recharge in the low polders → Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders).

Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011

attributes.label: Land subsidence
attributes.description: How fast the land surface of the island's polders falls. Peat above the groundwater compacts and its organic matter oxidises as it is drained (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 13, the board's rules for its whole area), and the fall adds up in Polder surface elevation. The island's low polders lie on peat: in Schouwen's low polder salt-marsh soils alternate with basin clay with peat (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 23), and under Duiveland a peat layer lies almost everywhere at −1.6 to −3.4 m NAP, under calcareous sand or light clay (2021a, p. 20), often within a metre of the surface in its low south and middle (p. 19). Drained by ditches, the polders have sunk over several hundred years as the peat compacted and the clay ripened (2021b, pp. 20, 22; 2021a, p. 18). No source read gives the rate on the island. The rate follows the drainage within the year, so an Auxiliary; what builds up slowly is the elevation, a Stock.
attributes.ask actors: Waterschap Scheldestromen, through DCC or Living Lab: How fast the island's polders subside, per area: the board changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 50).

attributes.label: Polder surface  elevation (NAP)
attributes.description: The land surface elevation of the island's polders relative to NAP, lowered by subsidence: most of the low polders' surface lies around NAP (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10), the western low polders mostly between −1 and −2 m NAP and the eastern ones at about 0 to +1 m (pp. 27–28), the middle and east of Schouwen between −1.5 and −0.5 m NAP (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 22), and Zeeland's lowest polders at −1.5 to −2.5 m relative to mean sea level (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661, for the province). Tidal silt, let in through a wisselpolder, would barely raise it on this island: the Grevelingen has no tide, and the Oosterschelde has too little silt to raise polders on a large scale (De Mesel et al., 2013). Since the storm surge barrier its channels carry 52–70% less suspended sediment (Ma et al., 2014, p. 15); near Zierikzee the water holds under 10 mg/l, presumably mostly fine sand, and on the Oosterschelde's salt marshes 3–10 mm settles a year, about −1 to 5 mm after compaction (van Maldegem & de Jong, 2004, pp. 14, 27–28), against 16–32 mm a year on young marshes along the Westerschelde in 1931–1955 and 4–18 mm in 1955–2002 (De Mesel et al., 2013, p. 25).

attributes.label: Root zone salinity
attributes.description: The salt concentration of the soil water in the crop root zone. Salt harms a crop in two phases: at once osmotically, slowing the growth of young leaves, and more slowly as sodium (Na+) or chloride (Cl-) builds up in the leaves, ageing the older ones early (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656, a review of plant physiology, which holds wherever the crop grows). It rises in a dry summer as the soil dries out and salt rises by capillary rise, and falls with the winter's rain surplus, which in one winter washes the topsoil of most well-drained soils free enough of salt to be cropped, and that of badly drained soil in two, exceptionally three (van Beekom et al., 1953a, pp. 155–158, measured after the floods in Zeeland): within the year where the soil drains well, so an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources:

attributes.label: Saline seepage (kwel)
attributes.description: The upward flow of salt groundwater from the sand below into the clay and peat top layer of the island's polders, in mm a day, which leaves through drains, ditches and evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3662). The higher water pressure at depth drives it in the low polders, where it keeps the rainwater lenses thin, mostly under 2 m, and the shallow groundwater brackish to salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10); below the lens its water holds 10 to 16 g of chloride a litre (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675), against about 16 to 17 g in North Sea water (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Most of Duiveland gets salt seepage, most in its low parts near the Oosterschelde (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 27); in the western low polders it is strongest near the Grevelingen and the Oosterschelde (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The flow follows the water pressures, which change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Soil structure
attributes.description: The soil's aggregates and pores, which set how fast water soaks in: well-drained clay with its structure intact let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely, while clay whose structure sodium had broken down became impervious and sticky when wet (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, pp. 230, 233, measured after the floods in Zeeland). A Stock: once broken down, it recovers over years (Root zone salinity → Soil structure). Workability, which structure and wetness both shape, is Spring workability of the fields.

attributes.label: Upconing of salt  groundwater
attributes.description: The rise of salt groundwater towards a well that pumps fresh water from a lens floating on it, in a cone under the well. In Zeeland fresh groundwater is mostly pumped through horizontal wells, under rules meant to limit this upconing and salt intrusion (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 1). In the Freshmaker pilot on a creek ridge at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the pumped water grew saltier during each pumping season, which the report explains by the lens thinning and the cone possibly reaching the shallow well (p. 67); in a model of the creek ridge at Serooskerke, Walcheren, the cone had not settled after ten years (p. 58), the slow part being the lens itself (Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges, a Stock). The island's creek ridges hold the same kind of lens, rain soaked in over salt groundwater (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Deltares, modelling Zeeland's rules in 2018, found that on the whole they seem enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around a well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, answer 3). Within the season: an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Farmers' demand for  deep polder drainage
attributes.description: Farmers' wish for low ditch levels, so that their fields drain: dry enough for heavy machinery to work them, which holding water back for dry times sometimes makes hard (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44), and free of water damage after heavy rain, which farmers in the island's western low polders often find a bigger problem than drought (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). They put it to the water board as it prepares its water level plans, which it does with interest groups such as farming, and in views on a draft (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17): on Duiveland's draft of 2021, four views feared that a raise the plan proposed to study would bring more flooding in extreme rain (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53). Within the year, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Fresh water supplied  to the island
attributes.description: Fresh water brought to the island's farms from outside it in the growing season (present in Tholen and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen; absent on Walcheren, the Bevelanden and Schouwen-Duiveland). It needs a supply route, and in drought it is what the national distribution leaves for the route to carry. Rijkswaterstaat makes that distribution: in drought it divides the little fresh water of the large rivers and lakes among the users through weirs, pumping stations and sluices, by the verdringingsreeks when there is too little for all, and the greater part of Zeeland lies outside the area it can supply (Rijkswaterstaat, n.d.).
attributes.sources: Rijkswaterstaat. (n.d.). Verdeling water bij droogte. Retrieved November 6, 2026, from https://www.rijkswaterstaat.nl/water/waterbeheer/droogte-en-watertekort/verdeling-water-bij-droogte

attributes.label: Freshwater  availability for crops
attributes.description: Fresh water crops can draw on in the growing season: rain, the soil moisture and groundwater of the field above the lens, water farmers pump or have stored, and water supplied from outside, which reaches the island nowhere now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 8). A Stock: water held in the root zone and in storage carries over from day to day: the root zone's is a daily balance, what the day before left plus rain, irrigation and capillary rise, less what the crop uses and what drains below the roots (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 85). It fills and empties within the season.

attributes.label: Freshwater storage  measures
attributes.description: The fresh water a year that the measures in place on the island's farms keep, store or collect for the growing season. They work three ways (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 16–23, 53, for the island): in the low polders, controlled drainage and anti-salinisation drainage (Drains2Buffer) keep the thin rainwater lens against salt, their water staying in the field's own soil, where it cannot be pumped (pp. 33, 53), and weirs in ditches keep the lens in flat areas drained by ditches with a moderate to large drooglegging (pp. 16, 19); on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay, the creek-ridge infiltration system, the Freshmaker and underground storage under a clay layer infiltrate winter water to pump in summer (pp. 20–22, 38); and double drainage, a concept the study shows only in model simulations, not yet tested in practice, would collect fresh drain water into a basin to irrigate from (pp. 23, 29, 32). An adaptive practice: measures to keep more fresh water in the ground as drought and salinisation increase (p. 4). The study set out from their being not yet fitted to the island and too risky for many farms to invest in alone (pp. 4, 11), and concluded that more is possible than the farmers first thought (pp. 5, 55). A Stock: a measure, once built, lasts 15 to 30 years (pp. 17–22, 34). The farm decides a measure; infiltrating water needs the water board's permit or a notification, a weir the neighbours' consent, and raising a ditch's level the water board's cooperation (pp. 26, 44–45). Whether a farm wants to store weighs storing against its other ways through a dry summer (pumping, other crops), where capacity to invest is whether it can. Stored water pays back over years, which suits a farm that owns its land more than one on a short lease; and where stored water spreads under the neighbours, one farm pays and others gain. Whether either holds a farm back is a question for the group model building session. Beside the farms, Acacia Water, Deltares and Delphy shape it: in a demonstration with the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality, double drainage was laid on two test plots at Kerkwerve and anti-salinisation drainage on one at Dreischor, on three of the island's farms (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2023), the EU's rural development programme paying half of the cost and the knowledge parties a part of it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b). Measures of these kinds are among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013: drains set deeper or regulated, a deep drain for salt, a storage basin, extraction from creek ridges and injection into a deep aquifer.
attributes.simplification: Counts the measures of three kinds as one quantity, the fresh water a year they keep, store or collect, each kind reaching crops by its own link out: to Winter rain drained away, to Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes, and to Freshwater availability for crops. It assumes every kind responds alike to the drivers into this element. Every loop through it keeps its polarity and its mechanism; what it leaves out is that a rise in one kind need not be a rise in another, so the semi-quantitative analysis cannot vary them apart.

attributes.label: Groundwater extraction  for irrigation
attributes.description: Fresh water farmers pump from the fresh groundwater through their own wells, to irrigate in summer; the water board's pumping stations belong to drainage. How much and from where is Pumping the water board allows. Whose lens a well draws on, the farm's own or one it shares with its neighbours, so that a farm pumping less leaves water to them, is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the rules are written so that a well's effects stay within the farm's own field (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021), an aim of the rules rather than a measurement. Irrigation and a well into a phreatic aquifer are among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013. Pumping follows the season's shortfall within the year: an Auxiliary.

attributes.description: The views and appeals against the plans for the island's water and land while a plan is pending, the water board's level plans among them, which can slow, change or stop it. attributes.label: Winter rain drained  away
attributes.description: Rain in winter that field drains carry off instead of refilling the rainwater lens: tile drains usually discharge shallow groundwater rapidly during rain, as other studies found (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661), and on Schouwen-Duiveland a large part of the year's rain is drained away in the wet season (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 54). It follows each rain, within the year: an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Crop yield
attributes.description: Physical yield per hectare of conventional crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) under the prevailing freshwater, soil and workability conditions; what salt takes from their harvest is Harvest lost to salt. The island's arable farms grow potatoes, onions, sugar beet, cereals, grass seed and vegetables in rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30, 38, from the farms studied), and some in the low polders have stopped growing sown onions for the salt (p. 31). A season's harvest: an Auxiliary.
attributes.simplification: The current crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) are one yield per hectare. Each yields less with a larger water shortfall, worse soil structure or fields that cannot be worked in time, so every link into the yield keeps its sign for each crop and no loop through it changes. What one yield leaves out: the crops lose in different proportions (the yield response factors on Crop water shortfall → Crop yield), and farms can shift their rotation among them, as some in the low polders stopped growing sown onions for the salt.

attributes.label: Market demand for  alternative crops
attributes.description: Consumer demand and offtake contracts for novel salt-tolerant or alternative crops (e.g. protein crops). For quinoa the market is small: in Flanders it is sold under contract at €1,100 a tonne on a local market still very limited, with no forecast yet of how demand for local quinoa will grow (Cloet et al., 2024, pp. 2–3); in the Netherlands a supermarket has its own-brand quinoa from 12 Dutch farmers under a three-year contract, Dutch quinoa costing more to buy in than imported (DutchNews.nl, 2026). For protein crops, Rabobank expects demand for plant-based meat and dairy alternatives to grow towards 2030, while yields lower than in other countries and a quality that often misses food standards, which keeps the price low, limit what they earn (Polman et al., 2026, p. 8). For halophytes such as samphire and sea aster, grown in a few places in Zeeland, the food market is small and easily saturated, and offers farmers no lasting market potential (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6). Measured in Flanders, the Netherlands and Zeeland, none on the island.

attributes.label: Local processing  capacity for new crops
attributes.description: Plants and supply chains on or near the island that store, process or sell new salt-tolerant crops. Breeding of tolerant varieties is Salt-tolerant varieties on offer. No source read shows a new crop processed on the island. Sea vegetables are sorted and packed, mostly by hand, by a grower and trader at Nieuw- en Sint Joosland, who in 2018 shipped most of his sea fennel, seaweed and sea spaghetti to organic shops and was investing, with a colleague from Schouwen-Duiveland, in growing new sea greens in greenhouses to supply international restaurants and supermarkets directly (FreshPlaza, 2018); at Colijnsplaat an arable farmer and a trader of sea vegetables founded a company, NZZT, to grow sea crops and set up their supply chain, in a project of 2020–2021 (EU CAP Network, 2023). GreenFood50 runs its quinoa chain, from grower to customer, from Wageningen, and has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities (GreenFood50, n.d.), and a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a). Buyers and processors build or keep it where they find it worthwhile against processing the crops elsewhere.

attributes.label: Adoption of new  salt-tolerant crops
attributes.description: Hectares under crops new to the island's rotations that tolerate salt. On the parcels studied in the island's low polders the rotations hold potato, onion, sugar beet, cereals and grass seed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30), and no source read shows a new crop grown on the island. Elsewhere in Zeeland, most still experimental and small (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 57): samphire and sea aster, irrigated with saline water on the edges of salt marshes at Emmadorp, Waterdunen and Wolphaarsdijk, labour intensive and seasonal, their sales low (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6); sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat, where a new company worked out how to grow them, in fields and greenhouses, and set up their supply chain (EU CAP Network, 2023). Quinoa grows to maturity on irrigation water of more than 250 mM NaCl (van Loo, 2023, p. 77) and is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine, but needs a fine seed bed and weed control set by its row distance (p. 75). Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against their current crops; capacity to invest is whether they can, and dependence on the current crops what holds them. Switching to salt- or drought-resistant crop types is among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013. A Stock: a field keeps its crop through the season, and farmers move fields to a new crop over years, as they come to see the damage over dry summers (Harvest lost to salt → Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops).

attributes.label: Agricultural land  value
attributes.description: The price unlet farmland on the island sells for (€/ha), set by what buyers expect to earn from it. A buyer bids at most what an extra hectare can earn back over the years of the investment (Farjon et al., 2013, box Maximale biedprijs), and the price is set for an important part by what expanding farms earn on extra hectares, their income and expectations combined with what they can borrow: scale enlargement and low interest rates hold it up, swings in what the land earns and limits on banks' financing of land press it down (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 1–3). So the price of farmland in the Netherlands has risen far faster than what the land earns on average: the nominal price more than tenfold since 1970, net value added two to three times (Farjon et al., 2013, introduction). Farmers bought 54% of the land traded in the Netherlands from 2012 to early 2023 and investors 9%, whose purchases, as a share of the farmland, are highest in Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Zeeland; in Zeeland on average just over 1.5% of the farmland is sold on the free market in a year (Kuiper et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, Appendix 1). Banks hold it as security for their loans (Farjon et al., 2013, section Financiering van bedrijfsuitbreiding). No source read gives the island's land prices.
attributes.simplification: A soil's structure enters the land's value only through what the land earns (Soil structure → Crop yield → Farm income → this element), the sign the same, since buyers price what they expect it to earn. What it leaves out: any value a buyer gives good soil beyond its income.

attributes.label: Risk premium on farm  loans
attributes.description: The part of a farm loan's interest that differs between clients: the specific premium a bank charges above the base rate, which banks also call the credit or risk premium. The loan's risk sets it for a large part: the interest holds, per client, the bank's expected losses on the loan and the cost of the capital the banks' solvency rules require it to hold against it, both higher the higher the credit risk the bank sees; on a loan with a fixed rate it may be part of one total rate (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). No source read gives the premiums banks charge the island's farms.

attributes.label: Basel IV capital  requirements
attributes.description: The capital European rules require banks to hold against their loans, by the final Basel III standards. The EU sets them: its banking package (CRR III/CRD VI) puts the final elements of the Basel III standards of 2017 into EU law, the new rules of the Capital Requirements Regulation applying from 1 January 2025, those of the directive once each member state has transposed them; its output floor sets a lower limit on the capital requirements banks calculate with their own models; and environmental, social and governance risks enter the banks' handling of risk, the supervisors' annual review and disclosure (European Commission, Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union, 2023). By the EBA's estimate, EU banks' minimum Tier 1 capital requirement is 9.0% higher at full implementation in 2028, the output floor and credit risk contributing most (European Banking Authority, 2023). No source read shows climate or salinisation risk in the risk weights of farm loans.

attributes.label: Dependence on  high-margin  salt-sensitive crops
attributes.description: The share of the rotation under the high-value cash crops salt harms most, seed and ware potatoes and sown onions (Root zone salinity → Harvest lost to salt). Potatoes are financially attractive and sensitive to the climate, the most important crop of Dutch arable farming (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 12): on specialised arable farms on clay growing ware potatoes they bring in, on average over the years, 55% of the arable revenue, ware potatoes 32% and seed potatoes 23%, against 14% for onions and 11% for sugar beet (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 14). In Zeeland, a manager of the cooperative CZAV says, a farmer earns his money not with rotation crops but with onions, beets and potatoes (Economic Board Zeeland, 2023, p. 19). The guideline is potatoes on a field at most one year in three, against potato cyst nematode (one in two for starch potatoes), so a farm growing more of them rents or swaps land (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 4). On the parcels studied in the island's low polders, where the seepage pressure is high and the surface water salty all year, the rotations hold potato, onion, sugar beet, cereals and grass seed, the farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions, and with more fresh water they would be open to more profitable crops (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30–31). In Zeeland the sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 in 2024 after dry summers, poor harvests and a lack of fresh water, which four in five arable farmers have no access to, while potatoes held at about 19,000 ha (De Vriend, 2024b). A Stock: the share holds through the season and shifts over years (Root zone salinity → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops).

attributes.label: Farm income
attributes.description: Farms' income from their crops: the revenue from crop sales, set by yield and prices, minus the costs they pay (rent, interest, the water board's levy, their own pumping) and depreciation, as Dutch farm accounts measure it (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), per hectare in a year. Dutch arable farms earned about 65,000 euro per unpaid labour unit on average over 2010–2016, spread widely: in 2016 a fifth had a negative income and as many earned more than 100,000 euro (pp. 21–22). In 2025 an estimated 60,000 euro, lower prices after good harvests in north-west Europe and beyond outweighing the yields (van der Meulen, 2025). No source read gives the island's farm incomes.

attributes.label: Farmers' capacity to  invest
attributes.description: What a farm can put into an investment: its savings, built up from what is left of its income after the household's spending and its payment obligations, repayments included, and the credit a bank will give it. A farm whose income is negative cannot reserve enough for investment (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 25), and one short of cash first cuts maintenance and private spending or draws on its savings, and if that is not enough can ask its bank to defer part of its interest and repayments or for more credit (p. 28); banks judge more and more whether a farm's operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Machines, implements and installations are the main category of Dutch arable farms' investment (p. 19), and irrigation systems cost relatively much to install, not always within a farmer's reach (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28).

attributes.label: Financial leverage
attributes.description: The farm's debt relative to the value of its assets, the inverse of its solvency (equity as a share of total capital). Land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), so the ratio moves with the land price: arable farms' solvency was 81% in 2018 because their land had risen in value, while their long-term debt had tripled since 2001 to 770,000 euro per farm, and it differs widely between farms (p. 21). Farms that expanded recently have a lower solvency, and large arable farms, of about 190 ha on average in 2015, about 70% against 80% for arable farming as a whole in 2010–2015 (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); farms that own little of their land gain little from a rising land price but owe much less (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26).
attributes.actors: Banks lending to the island's farmers

attributes.label: Arable land in the  polders
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's land under arable crops, the census's akkerbouw, conventional or salt-tolerant and fallow included, whoever owns it: 9,094 ha in 2025 against 11,395 ha in 2000, on farms whose main seat is on the island (CBS, 2026). The farms growing them halved over those years, from 402 to 200, so the hectares per farm rose from 28 to 45: land from a farm that stops mostly goes in parts to neighbouring farms that are expanding, which can pay the most for it (Luijt, 2007, p. 25, nationally). The fall in hectares is net, the census's farmland 906 ha smaller and its grass and forage crops 1,431 ha larger (CBS, 2026). It falls when the land's holder, present or next, stops growing arable crops on it; what the land becomes then (nature, grassland, water storage) waits for the group's system boundary.

attributes.label: Crop water shortfall
attributes.description: What crops need in the growing season beyond the water they get: the gap farmers' water decisions respond to. What a crop needs, whatever the water's origin, is the water it uses when it has enough, its evapotranspiration, set by the weather (radiation, air temperature, humidity and wind speed) and by the crop and its stage of growth (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56, a guide to crop water use that holds wherever the crop grows). The island's farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders; with no link to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought in and no ditches flushed in dry periods, so the farms run short of water, as the dry years 2018, 2019 and 2020 showed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: ZLTO's call for a  supply route
attributes.description: How firmly ZLTO asks the province, the municipality and the water board for a route bringing fresh water to the island. After a report on the island's freshwater demand, its branch there called a pipeline from the Haringvliet the one solution (Omroep Zeeland, 2023), and its chair looks for more fresh water with the municipality and the province (van Essen, 2026). An Auxiliary: it follows the shortfall farmers report and holds nothing of its own.

attributes.label: Freshwater supply  route to the island
attributes.description: Pipes or channels that could bring fresh water to the island, as their capacity in a summer; none exists. Provincie Zeeland, the actor here as the only body shown acting on the island's route, had a pipeline explored after the farming sector pressed for one (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 7); the study leaves open who pays and who would run it (p. 51), and no source read shows a decision. Once one is decided on, the study expects implementing the main supply pipeline to take about 3 to 10 years depending on the variant, and the distribution on the island within 2 to 3 years by a ring pipeline or about 5 to 10 years through watercourses that need widening, naming the time needed for permits, land acquisition and further engineering among what lengthens it (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, pp. 43–44, 46–47). By law a project decision can come from the water board's executive, for its water tasks, the province's or a minister (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 5.44), and the water board may charge the farmland a supply project serves up to 100% more, once at least half of its owners have responded and two thirds of those are in favour (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 122); it charges more for its supply projects on Tholen and Sint Philipsland and in the Reigersbergsche polder (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026c, arts. 5–6). IenW shapes it twice: its minister allots the Delta Fund, from which a freshwater region can claim 25% of a regional measure's cost, in principle up to 50% for an innovative one or one carried out by several regions (Algemene Rekenkamer, 2026, p. 32); and the Delta Programme 2027, under the Delta Commissioner's direction and presented by the minister with the Delta Fund's budget, proposes that the south-west delta's areas with no supply from outside speed up their way to self-sufficiency, the region open to exploring small extensions of the supplied area that add evident value, are future-proof and keep the extra demand on the Volkerak-Zoommeer limited, the demand on the Hollandsch Diep and Haringvliet not raised (Ministerie van Infrastructuur en Waterstaat et al., 2026, pp. 4, 88–89).

attributes.label: Spring workability of  the fields
attributes.description: Whether heavy machinery can work the fields early in spring without damaging the soil, set by soil structure and by how wet the soil is: soil work done when the soil is too wet can smear and compact it and form clods, by the Dutch cultivation guide, and in the climate scenarios more rain in spring leaves fewer moments to do it (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, on potatoes). It follows the soil's wetness within the season, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Polder drainage depth
attributes.description: How far below the surface the water board holds the ditch levels in the island's polders (the drooglegging), as its water level plans set them: Duiveland's plan sets a target level for each of its level areas, from 0.8 to 2.7 m below NAP, in most the summer level higher than the winter one, against nature's order, to prevent water damage in winter and drying in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 64–65). It moves from the winter level to the summer one in steps in March and April, as the weather and the farmers' soil work allow (p. 66). On a creek ridge studied for water storage the depth is over 1.5 m in winter in large parts (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 42). The depth holds until the board carries out a new plan: Duiveland's study of 2021 drew up a new plan to replace the one in force since 1982 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 5, 24), and the board checks each plan every three years and renews it at 17 years or once it no longer fits (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17), so a Stock. Where the land subsides under a level held, the depth shrinks until a new plan lowers the level, as the board's policy describes for peat (2025, p. 13).

attributes.label: Water board's plans to  raise ditch levels
attributes.description: The water level plans in which Waterschap Scheldestromen raises a polder's ditch levels, from the draft until their levels take effect. The board matches its levels to the land's use and soil, its principle that the level follows the land use: arable land 60 to 120 cm below the surface by soil, permanent grassland as a rule 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29; 2025, pp. 5, 7, 19), weighing flooding, drought, fresh water and groundwater (2021c, p. 19), subsidence (2025, pp. 13–14) and a change's costs against its benefits (2025, p. 12). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, where levels had been kept low to store extreme rain, to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (2021a, p. 69). The general board adopts each plan (2025, p. 18); of its 30 members, 26 represent the residents and two the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, appointed by ZLTO's board (Reglement voor het Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, arts. 6–7). A plan waits years for the works its levels need (Water board's plans to raise ditch levels → Polder drainage depth), so a Stock.
attributes.simplification: The two seats on the general board for the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, were a Constant driving these plans, and are in the description instead: no loop runs through a Constant, so no loop changes. What it leaves out: the seats cannot be set as an input of their own.

attributes.label: Water board's pumping  costs
attributes.description: What Waterschap Scheldestromen spends on electricity for the pumping stations that hold the polders' ditch levels, by pumping out the water that reaches the ditches. Every polder on the island is pumped: on Schouwen all water flows to two pumping stations, which pump it over the dike into the Oosterschelde and the Grevelingen (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 24); low-lying Duiveland has a pumping station for each of its five drainage areas (2021a, p. 21). Across the board's area the cost follows the water pumped: in the dry year 2025 its water systems spent €1.1 million less on electricity than budgeted, for the drought (2026e, p. 18), and for 2026 it budgets about €4.8 million for the electricity of its sewage and polder pumping stations together, which extreme rain can raise by up to 25% (p. 55). No source read gives the island's share. A year's spending: an Auxiliary.
attributes.simplification: Draws only the water coming in: Saline seepage and Winter rain drained away, which Polder drainage depth and Polder surface elevation already drive with the same sign, so every loop keeps its polarity. What it leaves out: how high the water is lifted, on which no source read shows the costs depending.
attributes.ask actors: Waterschap Scheldestromen, through DCC or Living Lab: What its pumping stations on the island use in electricity a year, how much of the water they pump is seepage and how much rain, and how far the cost depends on how high they lift it: on Duiveland it measures the discharge at each pumping station (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 24).

attributes.description: What Waterschap Scheldestromen charges on farmland for its water management, pumping included. attributes.label: Harvest lost to salt
attributes.description: The conventional crops' harvest that salt in the root zone takes, over the island's fields still under them, in a season. On the island, farms where seepage pressure is high and the surface water is salty all year have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Zeeland is among the coastal provinces where potatoes and barley lose considerable yield to salt (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). Salt's effect on yield builds up over weeks to months and is read over the season (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Margin given up on  high-margin crops
attributes.description: On the hectares a farm moves from its high-margin current crops, potatoes and sown onions, to new salt-tolerant crops or to salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops: what the current crop would earn without salt less what the new crop or variety earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1). What salt takes is Harvest lost to salt, so it is not counted here. Potatoes, beets, onions and field vegetables are the high-margin crops; the margin of protein crops is comparable to that of cereals and cannot compete with most other crops (Polman et al., 2026, p. 9); quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small, against cultivation costs under contract of about €1,470 a hectare, storage and marketing left out (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 2). In the Netherlands, interviews on quinoa and seed potatoes on saline soil found the lack of economic benefits the main constraint on scaling them (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 276), and on Terschelling food grown on salt-affected soil costs more to produce than food grown with fresh water, the project relying on volunteers and, at its start, on subsidies (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 13, 16). A season's crop: within the year.

attributes.description: Arable farms on the island whose farmer has someone to take the farm over. Nationally, in 2023, 43% of the 33,000 farms whose head is over 50 had a successor, against 40% in 2020, and 39% of the arable farms, the agricultural census asking three times in ten years (Agrimatie, 2024); no source read gives the island's figure.

attributes.description: The volume of new salt-tolerant crops harvested in a year within reach of a processor or trader on or near the island, from the island's growers and from growers elsewhere. Quinoa has been grown in Zeeland since 2016, on one to four parcels a year at six locations in all (Bogers et al., 2025, pp. 28, 38), its map showing one of them on the island, while the growers who sell to GreenFood50 in the Netherlands farm about 200 hectares for 600 tonnes a year (DutchNews.nl, 2026); samphire, from Zeeland and France, is by far the main product of a Zeeland trader in sea vegetables (FreshPlaza, 2018).

attributes.label: Adoption of  salt-tolerant  varieties
attributes.description: Hectares under salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops (potato, onion), which use the same machines, storage and know-how. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against the variety they grow now. Such potato varieties exist and are tested in the Netherlands: of 13 cultivars from Dutch breeders and suppliers grown in the field on Texel from 2012 to 2018, Elgar and Rivola kept 90% of their yield up to a soil salinity above 7.5 dS/m, against 4 to 4.5 dS/m for five others (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 2, 10); for onion, no source read shows one variety more tolerant than another. No source read shows them grown on the island or in Zeeland: stakeholders in the Dutch potato industry named salt-tolerant varieties as developed in the Netherlands mostly for arid countries, with no mention of domestic use (Aldrich et al., 2023, p. 38). Switching to salt- or drought-resistant varieties is among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013. A Stock: a field keeps the variety sown in it for the season, so the hectares hold until farmers sow again.

attributes.label: Salt-tolerant  varieties on offer
attributes.description: Salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops that breeders bring to market, and their yield; breeding lies outside the CLD's scale. Dutch breeders and suppliers sell potato cultivars that differ in salt tolerance: of 13 bought from them and tested in the field on Texel, Rivola, Elgar and '927' were more tolerant than the others on sandy soil (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 2, 11). With no official label for salt tolerance, trading houses claim it for no variety and only say which suit saline soils best and worst, and salt tolerance is not yet among the ten traits their salespeople rank most important for a new variety (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 271–272); stakeholders interviewed in the Dutch potato industry say the salt-tolerant seed potatoes bred in the Netherlands are mostly for export to arid countries such as Egypt and Morocco (Aldrich et al., 2023, pp. 38, 40). Tolerant varieties yield relatively little against common high-yielding ones without salt or under mild salt, and conventional breeding typically takes 10 to 15 years (van den Burg et al., 2024, pp. 3, 6). Measured in interviews across the Dutch potato chain and in field trials on Texel; none on the island.

attributes.label: Machines and storage  for the current crops
attributes.description: The machines a farm owns that suit only one or a few crops (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45) and the buildings, machines and paving for storing its potatoes and onions (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), a store for long keeping being a mostly insulated building with a cooling installation (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 5). Nationally an estimated 1,500 farms at least, mainly arable ones, had a store for long keeping with potatoes still in it on 1 April 2020, which takes a cooled store; taken as all arable, that is 40% of the 3,725 specialised arable farms growing ware potatoes (p. 7). Machines are depreciated at 8.2% a year, installations at 10% and buildings at 3% (p. 13, from KWIN 2018): about 12, 10 and 33 years, if that is a constant share of the purchase price. Machines, implements and installations are the main category of Dutch arable farms' investment (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). No source read counts them on the island, where one farmer interviewed names mechanisation among the reasons for adding land (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57).

attributes.label: Capital lost on  switching to new crops
attributes.description: What the machines, storage and know-how of a farm's current crops would stop earning if it moved fields to a crop that cannot use them, less what it can sell them for. A store's costs do not fall when the crops in it take a smaller part of the rotation: they are sunk and cannot be earned back (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), and other paths need new technology and skills while the old may not yet be written off (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). It differs by what the farm moves to. Quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine harvester (van Loo, 2023, p. 75); adding protein crops leaves buildings and machines as they were (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4), and a store stands idle only once nothing it can hold is grown. A salt-tolerant variety of a current crop is planted, lifted and stored as that crop is, so it loses little of it, which no source read states. No source read says what a used harvester or store would fetch.

attributes.label: Farmers' knowledge of  new crops
attributes.description: What the island's farmers know about growing and selling new salt-tolerant crops, from their own fields, their neighbours' and advisers. For quinoa this knowledge is still thin in the Netherlands: research on growing it is relatively underdeveloped, and a grower harvested 2,000 kg from 4 hectares one year and 2,500 kg the next without knowing why, multiple interviewees agreeing that too little is known (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 269); what Dutch consumers want from it is under-researched (p. 270). Knowing that crops must cope with salt is a separate matter: most of Zeeland's farmers know it, yet still grow common salt-sensitive crops such as potato and wheat (Stuyt et al., 2016, as cited in van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6). Measured in 32 interviews, 29 of them in the Netherlands and seven with farmers (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 266), and across Zeeland; none on the island.

attributes.label: Spending on keeping  the current crops
attributes.description: What farms invest a year in carrying on with their current crops: wells and irrigation, drains, new machines and stores. On Dutch arable farms the main category of investment is machines, implements and installations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19, from national farm accounts); in Zeeland fresh groundwater may as a rule be pumped only through horizontal wells, from a fresh body over 15 m thick outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26), and in a creek-ridge cluster's estimate a horizontal well for brackish water costs €25,000 to €40,000 (pp. 48–49); and most of the farmers in five quickscans on the island's eastern creek ridges have drains in part of their fields (p. 38). An Auxiliary: a year's spending, what it buys accumulating in Machines and storage for the current crops.

attributes.label: Banks' risk assessment  of farm loans
attributes.description: The risk a bank sees in lending to an arable farm: more and more whether its operations will earn enough over the longer term to meet all its financial obligations, the expected income the limiting factor, beside its solvency and its land and buildings as security (van der Meulen et al., 2020, pp. 19, 47; Farjon et al., 2013, section Financiering van bedrijfsuitbreiding). Because arable returns swing from year to year, banks count farm loans as riskier despite the land as security, and the Basel capital rules steer them further toward lending on profitability and liquidity rather than on the value of the collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47); financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven they often count as a risk (p. 6). Rabobank's provisions for expected credit losses carried an adjustment of 87 million euro for climate risk at the end of 2024, set by sector on five events, drought and water scarcity among them (Rabobank, 2025, pp. 246–247). A public plan that may change what a farm can earn enters it before the plan is decided (Water board's plans to raise ditch levels → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans). A Stock: a bank's view of a farm holds until the bank revises it, and it weighs what the farm can earn over the longer term rather than in one year (Farm income → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans).

attributes.label: Bank credit to farms
attributes.description: New loans and refinancing that banks grant the island's arable farms in a year. Banks supply 90% of Dutch farms' long-term loans (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 20), whose total rose from 18 to 33 billion euro between 2001 and 2018, falling slightly in its last years (p. 19), and they have raised the repayments on land loans, ABN AMRO cutting the longest term for new farmland financing from fifty to forty years, a repayment of at least 2.5% a year (p. 47). No source read gives the banks' lending on the island.

attributes.label: Debt payments
attributes.description: The interest, commission and repayments farms owe their banks in a year. Interest and commission cost Dutch farms about 22,000 euro each in 2018, down from 30,000 in 2014 as interest rates fell (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 20); on arable farms interest was 8% of the costs they paid in 2018, against 12% in 2001, 2006 and 2011 (p. 57). The repayment follows mainly from the loan's size, term and schedule (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), and banks have raised the repayments on land loans, ABN AMRO to at least 2.5% a year on new land loans (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). No source read gives the island's farms' payments.

attributes.label: World prices of  conventional crops
attributes.description: The prices of potatoes, onions and sugar beet on the markets the island's crops are sold on, which its farms cannot move: what carrying on is weighed against. They form in an international market by supply and demand (Minister van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, 2018), moved by the harvests of north-west Europe and beyond, whose good harvests lowered arable prices in 2025 (van der Meulen, 2025; for potatoes, Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). The Netherlands was the world's largest onion exporter in 2016, and by a rough estimate about 80% of Dutch onions are processed in Zeeland (Minister van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, 2018); onions are rarely sold under fixed-price contracts agreed in advance, so their price can swing (Bogosavac, 2018). The potato processors export an estimated 80% of their frozen products, and buy 90 to 95% of their potatoes under contract or in a pool, the rest free (Janssens et al., 2020, pp. 1, 7), a contract's base price published each year for four processors (p. 11). No source read here gives how the beet price is set.

attributes.label: Farmers' trust in  government
attributes.description: How far the island's farmers expect the public bodies that plan for its water and land to keep their commitments (compensation, their say over their land). Trust is typically created slowly and can be destroyed in an instant, and once lost may take a long time to rebuild (Slovic, 1993, p. 677, as a long-known quality of trust; Remkes, 2022, p. 19). No source read measures it on the island: in 2013, 141 farmers in the south-west Netherlands, 16 of the survey's 142 on Schouwen-Duiveland, averaged 2.64 on a seven-point scale of trust in their water board on drought (van Duinen et al., 2015b, pp. 745–749), and one submission to the Province in 2021, by an engineer (Ir.) arguing for a fresh Grevelingen lake, says the island's farmers no longer trust the Province, which it says still appears unwilling to act adequately on salinisation and is dragging its feet on fresh-water supply (Lases, 2021, p. 2). From outside the island's scale comes national policy changed or dropped: plans announced and then changed, postponed or stopped, which the National Ombudsman, from interviews with 32 farmers across the country, concludes has left the government unreliable for them (Nationale ombudsman, 2026, pp. 8, 15, 40), and a gap of trust with 'The Hague' (Remkes, 2022, p. 13). The same farmers feel that decisions about their farm, land or future are prepared elsewhere, that they can react only late or to a limited extent, and that policymakers ignore their input; the Ombudsman concludes that this leads to a lack of trust in government (Nationale ombudsman, 2026, pp. 24–25). Whether the island's farmers carry that over to the water board, the Province and the municipality, no source read shows: a question for the group model building session.

attributes.label: Expropriation of  farmland
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's farmland that a public body takes in a year for a use its plan sets, with full compensation, by an order a court must confirm. The municipal council, the water board for its water tasks, the Provincial Council and the minister can each give the order (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.4), and only for a use an adopted plan, a permit or a project decision allows, after a reasonable attempt to buy the land and with a start likely within three years (arts. 11.5–11.7, 11.11). On the island the State sought expropriation, in a draft decree, for a roundabout on the N59, of plots the decree does not say are farmland (Besluit rotonde N59, 2020, p. 3), and the municipal council gave an order, published in 2026 and still to be confirmed by the court, for a high-voltage station on a plan area wholly in agricultural use in 2023 (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026, p. 1; Braat, 2023, blad 9); no source read shows it there for water or nature, and the Province buys land for nature on a voluntary basis (Provincie Zeeland, Jaarstukken 2022, p. 4). Few cases reach a court, in the Krimpenerwaard 6 of 69 files (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10–11), since the threat mostly makes owners sell (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, section Context of the Study).
attributes.simplification: Counts every order as the municipality's, while the municipal council, the water board, the Provincial Council and the minister can each give one (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.4). Of the two orders read on the island, the municipal council gave the one for the high-voltage station (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026, p. 1); the one for the N59 roundabout came at the request of the Minister of Infrastructure and Water Management, under the law before the Omgevingswet, and carried out the municipality's land-use plan for the road (Besluit rotonde N59, 2020, p. 1). The CLD draws only the municipality's plans as what an order carries out (Farmland planned for other uses → Expropriation of farmland), so B14, the one named loop through it, keeps its polarity and its mechanism; what it leaves out is an order by another body for a plan of its own, which would lower trust the same way but close the loop through a plan the CLD does not draw.

attributes.label: Farmers' wish to keep  their land
attributes.description: How strongly farmers hold on to their land beyond its money value: family land, growing up on it. In the Krimpenerwaard, where a land-use plan designated farmland for nature with expropriation as its last step, owners who kept their land and turned it into nature themselves named the wish not to lose it, from an emotional bond with it, as an important reason, for one farm weighing more than moving (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 11, 49, 68); selling land held for generations often weighs heavily, though one farmer's father had advised getting out if he could (p. 54). At succession the farm customarily passes to one child at its low agricultural value, the other children giving up part of their inheritance so that the parental farm can continue (Luijt, 2007, pp. 23, 25). In interviews with 20 owners in the Netherlands facing a government plan on their land, owners described a strong emotional involvement in the plans, touching their social life and well-being, against government professionals who could end their work at five o'clock (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, pp. 172, 177). Measured among 14 owners interviewed in the Krimpenerwaard, dairy farms and private owners on peat, among 20 across the Netherlands, and nationally for succession; no source read measures it on the island or among arable farmers. Whether anything on the map moves it, at succession perhaps, is a question for the group model building session.

attributes.label: Farmland changing  hands
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's farmland sold, expropriated or passed on to a new holder in a year. Supply and demand come mainly from farmers, those who need land to expand and those who shed it as they downsize or end the farm, and together they set how much land is traded, its mobility, and at what price (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2). Over the long term the number of Dutch farms falls by 2 to 3% a year, mainly as farms end at the change of generation, the lack of a successor and a less favourable income outlook among the reasons (p. 2). Measured nationally; no source read gives the island's land sales.
attributes.actors: Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, Banks lending to the island's farmers

attributes.label: Farmland planned for  other uses
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's farmland that Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland's land-use plan (its omgevingsplan, with the changes it drafts to it) designates for a use other than arable farming, such as nature, water storage, housing or recreation. The municipal council adopts one omgevingsplan for the whole municipality, holding the rules a balanced allocation of functions to locations needs (Omgevingswet, 2026, arts. 2.4, 4.2); on the island all land-use plans of before merged into it when the law took effect on 1 January 2024, and in some cases the municipality can change it at the request of someone whose plan does not fit it (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.). How many hectares it designates for other uses, no source read gives. In the Krimpenerwaard, a municipal plan designating farmland for nature took from its preliminary draft in spring 2018 to irrevocable in October 2021, fifteen appeals against it reaching the Council of State (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 25). A Stock: the hectares stay designated until the council changes the plan, which takes years, and leave as the plan is carried out on them (Farmland planned for other uses → Arable land in the polders).
attributes.ask actors: Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, through DCC or Living Lab: How many hectares of the island's farmland the omgevingsplan designates for a use other than arable farming, and which changes to it the municipality is drafting.

attributes.label: Freshwater lens  thickness under creek  ridges and dunes
attributes.description: The thickness of the fresh groundwater under the island's sandy creek ridges and dunes, down to the middle of the mixing zone with the saline groundwater: 5 to 15 m under the creek ridges (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island), reaching about 30 m under the creek ridges and the dunes and nearly 100 m under the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). The lens farmers pump: wells are allowed only in fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick (p. 26), and farmers pump it through horizontal wells or deep drains to irrigate (pp. 20–22, 26, 38, 53). A Stock: it grows and thins over years (Freshwater storage measures → this lens).

attributes.label: Pumping the water  board allows
attributes.description: The volume the island's farms may pump a year under Waterschap Scheldestromen's rules. Where: from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). How: a horizontal well at most 6 m below the surface and 80 to 200 m long, at least 200 m from the next well and 50 m from a neighbour's field. How much: at most 800 m³ per hectare and 8,000 m³ per well a year, set by the balance between what rain recharges, the irrigation water and the extraction, so the fresh stock lasts and the fresh-salt boundary does not rise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 and its explanation). Extractions rose in recent dry years, and the province and the water board talk of registering the volumes more precisely (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021); no source read shows the farms' pumping changing the rules, the 2026 revision keeping the cap. A Stock: a notified well pumps until the board forbids it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b).

attributes.label: Knowledge of how  storage works on the  island
attributes.description: What the island's farmers, their advisers and contractors know of how freshwater storage works on the island: how the soil and groundwater behave, and what a measure costs, risks and yields. The knowledge from the pilots has not yet been translated to the island's soil, water and farm conditions, which leaves much uncertainty about building a measure, its costs, its management, its risks and its gain (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 11), and local advisers and farmers understand too little of how the soil and groundwater system works (p. 12). It builds up as measures are built and monitored, so a Stock. Outside the island's farms, the project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water shapes it, its final report by authors from Deltares, KWR, Acacia Water and Buro Waterfront (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 2–3): it drew up quickscan advice for 13 farmers (p. 9) and feasibility studies for clusters of farms (pp. 30, 33, 40), and made methods, maps and tools available with which farmers and advisers can go on by themselves (pp. 4, 55). The EU co-funded that project (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-a) and paid half of a later one, of Acacia Water, Deltares, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve, three farms and the municipality, which demonstrated and monitored new drainage on the island for figures and guidelines on building, managing and maintaining it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b); the programme of its closing meeting had Acacia Water, Deltares and Delphy explain its yield and effect (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2024).

attributes.label: Arable farmers on  Schouwen-Duiveland
attributes.interest: Enough fresh water when their crops need it, above all as they germinate, to lower their farms' risk or to raise production. Many want to invest in measures that hold fresh water, once the technique, its costs, its risks and its gain in yield are known for the island's conditions; while supply from outside and measures on the island are both still debated, they hold back.
attributes.influence: Decide what the island's farmland grows and how each field is drained, irrigated and supplied with water: in 2025, 200 farms registered on the island grew arable crops on 9,094 ha, of the 13,752 ha of farmland of its 240 farms. A measure in the subsoil can serve several neighbouring farms, which collect and tap its water together; the study of the island's farms explored measures for clusters of one to three. As owners of farmland they decide whether the water board may charge them more for a water supply project: at least half must respond and two thirds of those be in favour. On a draft water level plan they can send views within six weeks and, if affected, appeal at the court for six weeks after the decision. Score 5: they decide the adaptation itself.
attributes.affected: Their farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders: the island has no link to the main freshwater system, so in dry periods no water can be brought in and no ditches flushed, its shallow groundwater and ditches carry much salt, and the farms run short of water; drought in the growing season, subsidence and sea level rise make this worse, and the dry years 2018–2020 showed the farms vulnerable. Delphy's report on the island's freshwater demand (2023) finds farming on the island impossible without more fresh water; in 2026 a potato grower at Nieuwerkerk lost a fifth of his harvest to drought, had stopped growing onions for want of fresh water, and found ditch water at times nearly as salt as the Oosterschelde. Adapting is uncertain for them: the measures that store fresh water in the subsoil are not yet fitted to the island's conditions, their costs, risks and gain in yield unknown, so many farmers find the investment too risky to make alone.

attributes.label: Waterschap  Scheldestromen
attributes.interest: Safe dikes and dunes first; then an optimal use of the water system, its ditch levels matched to soil and land use, fresh water kept available where it can and fresh groundwater kept in stock, within costs society accepts. It has no task as a supplier of fresh water: measures beyond its regular water management are for the users of the fresh water to pay.
attributes.influence: Sets the island's ditch levels in its water level plans (peilbesluiten: Duiveland 2021, Schouwen 2022), for the waters the province designates, to be held as far as possible, matched as far as it can to soil type and land use such as farming, after a process with the people of the area; sets and enforces the rules for farms' groundwater extraction for irrigation in its waterschapsverordening, a notification within limits per hectare and per well, a permit beyond them. Its general board sets the levy that pays for its water management: for 2026 the owners of unbuilt land other than nature, farmland among them, carry 22.78% of the costs, at €115.53 a hectare, its base rate, with a higher one for paved public roads. It may charge the farmland a water supply project serves up to 100% more, once a stakeholder has asked for the project, at least half of the owners have responded and two thirds of those are in favour; it charges more for its supply projects on Tholen and Sint Philipsland (10 to 50%) and in the Reigersbergsche polder (35 to 45%). It can take project decisions and expropriate land for its water tasks only. Of the 30 seats on its general board, 26 are for residents, two for unbuilt land and two for nature. Score 5: it decides binding rules for the island's farms.
attributes.affected: Salinisation and drought enter its tasks: with sea level rise, drought and subsidence, more of its area may come to face salinisation; drought strengthens the harm saline seepage does, which is hard to undo; and drought, warming and salinisation affect the ecology of its waters. Dry springs and summers showed farming's need for fresh water in those seasons: supplying it is no legal duty of the board, yet a clear need in society, which it answers within its core tasks, using its surface water system to counter drought and keep fresh water available, exploring its treatment plants' effluent as a source and the sustainable use of fresh groundwater. Its budget for fresh water is limited, the costs fall to whoever benefits, and its legal means to charge them are limited. Farms' groundwater extraction asks more of its knowledge, monitoring, permits and enforcement, since extracting too much too fast draws up the salt water under the lenses; where too little fresh water is available, drying can damage roads, nature and dikes.

attributes.label: Gemeente  Schouwen-Duiveland
attributes.interest: A vital and liveable countryside, with farming, one of the island's main economic pillars, made climate-proof against salinisation, subsidence and extreme weather, and a reliable water system; water basins on farmland fitted into the landscape.
attributes.influence: Its council sets the omgevingsplan, since 1 January 2024 the one plan for the use of all land and buildings on the island, farmland included, and may expropriate land for a use that plan allows, where that is necessary and urgent, and establish a right of first refusal on land given a non-agricultural function; its executive decides where a farm may build a water basin outside its building plot; it pays part of farms' advice, research and machines for fresh water and climate-proof farming, and leads the Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland. Score 5: it decides binding plans for the island's farms.
attributes.affected: Salinisation, subsidence and extreme weather put pressure on farming, one of the island's main economic pillars, and with it on the vital and liveable countryside the municipality seeks to keep. It budgets €1.1 million for a new Living Lab programme (2025), so that the farm sector stays diverse and resilient; its subsidy for farms' advice, research and machines for fresh water opens on 1 October 2026. The water basins farms build against drought damage have a spatial impact on the landscape, so the municipality sets how a basin outside a building plot is fitted into it.

attributes.label: Provincie Zeeland
attributes.interest: Keeping agriculture in the delta, for the fertile deltas' part in world food production, and strengthening nature; enough fresh water and good water quality, worked out with stakeholders in the Zeeuws Deltaplan Zoet Water; groundwater extraction in balance with its recharge.
attributes.influence: Sets regional water policy and the omgevingsverordening, whose rules reach the water board, the municipalities, residents and businesses, among them instruction rules the water board's water level plans and the municipality's omgevingsplan follow; sets the water board's tasks and rules of organisation and supervises it, its executive able to annul any of the board's decisions; designates in the omgevingsverordening the waters that need a water level plan; grants the permits for groundwater extraction above 150,000 m³ a year, for drinking water and for open soil energy systems. It may take project decisions and, for a provincial interest or where that is efficient, expropriate land, and for a provincial interest establish a right of first refusal on land given a non-agricultural function. In its omgevingsverordening it may rank the uses within the two lowest categories of the verdringingsreeks; no source read shows Zeeland doing so. It commissioned a study of a fresh water pipeline to the island (2021), after the farming sector pressed for one; the study leaves open who pays and who would run it, and no source read shows a decision on a route. Score 5: it decides binding rules for the island's farms, mostly through the water board's and the municipality's decisions.
attributes.affected: Zeeland has very little supply of fresh water of its own and salinisation as a specific concern; climate change raises the chance that demand for fresh water outruns supply, with negative consequences for agricultural yields and nature values, against its aim of keeping agriculture in the delta. Long drought causes water shortages, and sea level rise more (saline) seepage. Farms' groundwater extraction bears on its policy of balance between extraction and recharge: it researches registering extractions and extends the groundwater monitoring network to follow the small fresh groundwater stocks better.

attributes.label: Banks lending to the  island's farmers
attributes.interest: Loans a farm can repay from its cash flow, with its land and other assets as security; an investment whose returns are not yet proven they often count as a risk. In Rabobank's words, to be a partner of the entrepreneur and help farmers invest in sustainability.
attributes.influence: Supply 90% of the borrowed capital of Dutch farms (2018), Rabobank about 85% of the lending to the Dutch food and agri sector (2021); they decide whether a farm gets a loan and at what rate, judging more and more by its cash flow and the entrepreneur, as the Basel capital rules steer them towards profitability and liquidity, with land still an important security, and they count sustainability in classifying a borrower. Measured nationally: no source shows the banks' shares on the island. Score 4: they decide credit many of the island's farms depend on, without binding them.
attributes.affected: Of the Netherlands' arable regions, the south-western clay region faces the greatest task with drought in Rabobank's research (2023), above all because Zeeland is relatively vulnerable to salinisation: the average arable farm's income has held up in dry years, higher prices outweighing lower yields, but farms with little access to fresh water or with salinisation problems can come under pressure, and less fresh water could force a switch to far costlier drip irrigation. Measured for the whole bank, Rabobank's provisions for expected credit losses carry an adjustment for rising climate and environmental risks, more probable and intense droughts and floods among them, €87 million at the end of 2024 (€14 million a year earlier), its climate-sensitive sectors judged on five events, drought and water scarcity among them; no source read shows the banks' risk on the island.

attributes.label: Buyers and processors  of the island's crops
attributes.interest: Raw material of the volume and quality their plants and customers need. Cosun Beet Company, owned by its growers as a cooperative, wants the most value from the beet and good long-term returns for its members, its production in balance with its sales; a potato processor secures its supply through contracts that fix a volume and often its price.
attributes.influence: Decide what they take from the island's farms, at what price and to what quality. Cosun Beet Company, part of Royal Cosun, the growers' cooperative that also owns the potato processor Aviko, processes all sugar beet grown in the Netherlands: it sets how much beet each member may deliver (for 2026 cut from 100% to 90% of the allocation, after high yields and with sales limited) and advises its growers field by field. The Dutch potato processing industry turns about 4 million tonnes of potatoes a year into frozen products, an estimated 80% of them exported; of the potatoes for the industry, 5 to 10% are sold free and the rest under contract or in a pool (2020, pp. 1, 7, 11–12), a contract fixing a quantity, a price or both, the common hectare-tonnage contract a volume per hectare besides the price, with bonuses for quality and grading and deductions for tare; Aviko, Farm Frites, Lamb Weston/Meijer and McCain are the processors whose contract prices are reported. Measured nationally: no source read shows which buyers take the island's potatoes, onions and vegetables, or their shares there. No source read shows a buyer building, keeping or closing a plant for new salt-tolerant crops on or near the island. Score 4: they decide the sales many of the island's farms depend on (in 2025, 120 of its 240 farms grew potatoes and 110 sugar beet), without binding them.
attributes.affected: In a drought their supply shrinks and its quality falls, measured nationally: in 2018 the Dutch harvest was expected to be 23% smaller for potatoes, 13% for sugar beet and 44% for onions than a year earlier (CBS's estimate from a survey of 5,000 farmers), and north-western Europe's potato yield at least 15 to 25% below the long-term average. About 80% of the Dutch potato crop is sold to processors under contract, at around nine cents a kilo in 2018, while free-market potatoes reached 30 cents; many growers expected not to deliver their contracted volume, and growers asked the processors to share the cost of extra irrigation and to accept force majeure, while the processors held that a grower under contract should irrigate. Processors want potatoes of at least 40 mm, which many would not reach, and the potatoes' very high dry matter risked damage at harvest. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects the buyers and processors.
