attributes.label: ZLTO
attributes.interest: The continuity of farming and horticulture and a future for farmers and growers. On the island, more fresh water: in its island branch's words (2023), catching more rain and a collective system that brings fresh water to the island, a pipeline from the Haringvliet shared among the farmers.
attributes.influence: The association of 11,500 farmers and growers in Zeeland, Noord-Brabant and Zuid-Gelderland, in 44 local branches that speak for their members to the municipality and the water board; its board appoints the two members for unbuilt land, farmland included, of the water board's general board of 30; it takes the initiative in the plan that carries out the Deltaplan Agrarisch Waterbeheer in Zeeland, with the water board and the province; on the island its branch looks for more fresh water with the municipality and the province, and Delphy's report on the island's freshwater demand (2023), whose conclusions the branch welcomed, finds that farming there becomes impossible without more fresh water. Its island branch has called a pipeline from the Haringvliet the one solution (2023). In Reimerswaal, elsewhere in Zeeland, a request from its local branch to the water board and the province (2020) started the study of an extended fresh water supply, and it is a party to the intention agreement on that supply (2025), leading the work of gaining the farmers' support for it. Score 3: it shapes the water board's, the municipality's and the province's decisions directly by representing farmers, binding none.
attributes.affected: Its members' farms bear the losses: in a ZLTO board member's words (2022), drought and heat would make Zeeland's potato harvest considerably smaller than normal, and the drought, the article adds, salinised farmland, which harms crops; its island branch's chair (2023) expects the farms still active there in 2030 to have almost no income. It answers by asking for fresh water collectively: storage for rain, and pipelines from the rivers to farmland, which need large investments and more from the national government.

attributes.label: Consumers
attributes.interest: Food that is affordable, tastes good, is safe and of a known origin: across the EU, cost (54%), taste (51%), food safety and origin (both 46%) are the factors most often chosen when buying food; in the Netherlands nutrient content comes first (62%), and its impact on the environment and climate is chosen by 29%, among the highest shares in the EU (2022).
attributes.influence: What they buy reaches the island's farms through the buyers and processors: in the Netherlands about 4 million tonnes of potatoes a year become about 2 million tonnes of frozen products, an estimated 80% exported, sold through catering and fast food worldwide; when these closed in the Covid-19 crisis (2020), the market for processing potatoes collapsed mid-season, with about 1.5 million tonnes left in growers' stores. Dutch household consumption of table potatoes fell 15% from 2014 to 2017, to 13 kg a person, and Dutch production of table potatoes with it, to about 450,000 tonnes a year. Measured nationally. Score 2: they shape the farms' decisions indirectly, through the buyers' demand.
attributes.affected: In the 2018 drought, measured nationally, the potatoes and onions in the shops were smaller but stayed on the shelves. Onions became dearer, a kilo sometimes 25 cents more (LTO Nederland), as their trade rarely uses fixed-price contracts; potatoes, mostly grown under delivery contracts at prices agreed in advance, hardly did, though Albert Heijn saw both slightly dearer, supply being scarcer while demand stayed the same. The supermarkets' trade association expected consumers to notice little and not to eat less. No source read traces an effect on consumers to salinisation on the island.

attributes.label: EU
attributes.interest: Through its Common Agricultural Policy: farmers supported and agricultural productivity improved, for a stable supply of affordable food, a reasonable living for farmers, action on climate change and the sustainable management of natural resources, and living rural areas and landscapes. Through its banking rules: a resilient banking sector, financial stability and stable funding of the economy.
attributes.influence: Its Common Agricultural Policy is managed and funded at European level from the EU budget, through two funds: the EAGF, for direct support and market measures, and the EAFRD, for rural development, €387 billion for 2021–2027. Each EU country draws up a national CAP Strategic Plan from the toolbox of measures the Commission provides, and its payments are managed nationally, in the Netherlands by RVO at the tariffs LVVN's minister sets. To receive EU income support, farmers must respect conditionality: the statutory management requirements, EU rules on public, animal and plant health, animal welfare and the environment that bind every farmer, and the good agricultural and environmental conditions that bind those receiving CAP support; a farmer who violates them has the support reduced. EU funding for rural development co-funded the Living Lab's Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022) and paid half of its drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). Its banking package (CRR III/CRD VI) puts the final elements of the Basel III standards of 2017 into EU law, the new Capital Requirements Regulation rules applying from 1 January 2025. Score 5: it decides binding rules for the island's farms, through conditionality.
attributes.affected: In the Commission's words (2025), water scarcity already affects 30% of Europe's land area every year, and extreme weather, persistent droughts among it, will only worsen as the effects of climate change grow, affecting citizens, agriculture, the environment and businesses, with effects on health and on the supply of energy, food and drinking water, and leading more and more to economic losses across the EU. Its Water Resilience Strategy (2025) answers with, among other measures, a recommendation to improve water efficiency in the EU by at least 10% by 2030, each Member State setting its own targets, and a strengthened real-time early-warning and monitoring system for floods and droughts. Measured EU-wide: no source read shows how salinisation on the island affects the EU.

attributes.label: LVVN
attributes.interest: Sustainable, sufficient and safe food on everyone's plate, valuable nature and a vital countryside, for present and future generations. Agriculture, nature and food quality strengthen each other and sometimes chafe; it makes those dilemmas open to discussion and looks for ways forward together with others in society.
attributes.influence: Makes national policy, laws and rules for agriculture, fisheries, food and nature, whose compliance the NVWA supervises. Its minister sets the tariffs of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy support in the Netherlands: for 2025, €174 per hectare of basic income support, €50.35 more on a farm's first 40 hectares, and an eco-scheme premium of €60, €100 or €200 per hectare. RVO pays them out on its behalf to the farms that apply, in 2026 the eco-scheme premium for activities serving climate, soil and air, water, landscape and biodiversity, to a farm that keeps to the CAP's conditionalities. It publishes the Delta Programme with IenW and VRO, has directors on the Bestuurlijk Platform Zoetwater that advises the minister of IenW on the Delta Programme for Fresh Water, and with IenW and STOWA had a knowledge programme on salt in agriculture, nature and water management drawn up by Deltares, KWR and others, on the salt tolerance of crops among its questions: its plan estimates €760,000 for the first year, and €400,000 was available in 2025 to start carrying it out. Measured nationally: no source read shows its payments on the island. Score 3: it funds the island's farms directly, through the CAP payments.
attributes.affected: Drought and salinisation hit the farming its policy is for. Measured nationally by the Algemene Rekenkamer (2026), over 1998–2023, drought lowers the yield of potatoes by 1 to 2.1% a year on average, of arable vegetables, mainly onions, by 1.1 to 2.7%, of cereals by 0.9 to 2.1% and of sugar beet by 1.5 to 1.6%, from the province with the least damage to the one with the most; for ware potatoes the national 2.1% came in 2023 to 70.5 million kg and €14 to €35 million less; and drought raises salinisation, with effects on agriculture and nature. With IenW and STOWA it had a knowledge programme on salt drawn up (2025), because the growing salinisation of water and soil, partly through climate change, raises questions that need fundamental gaps in knowledge filled: how salty the soil moisture becomes, and how salt-tolerant crops are under Dutch conditions: when salt damages them and how far they recover. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects LVVN.

attributes.label: IenW
attributes.interest: A reachable country with strong dikes, where people stay safe and get from A to B, with clean air, soil and water, its living environment cared for and raw materials used sparingly. For fresh water, the goal it set with the regional governments in 2019: in 2050 the Netherlands is resilient against freshwater shortage.
attributes.influence: Responsible for national water policy, the safety, quality and availability of water among it, and for the working of Dutch water management as a whole; manages the main water system, the large rivers, lakes and seas, with Rijkswaterstaat carrying it out; may instruct provinces and water boards on regional water management where international obligations or interests beyond a region require it. Its freshwater policy ranks the uses of water in a shortage by the verdringingsreeks, which every water manager follows: agriculture in the last of its four categories, temporary irrigation of capital-intensive crops one higher. Its minister coordinates the Delta Programme for Fresh Water, which the six freshwater regions carry out, and manages the Delta Fund, which pays all of Rijkswaterstaat's freshwater measures in the main water system and 25% of a region's (up to 50% for innovative ones or those of several regions): just over €58 million for fresh water in 2026; early in 2027 the Rijk and the regions set the measures for 2028–2033. The Delta Programme 2027, which its minister presents to parliament with the Delta Fund's budget, proposes for the south-west delta that the areas with no supply from outside speed up their way to self-sufficiency, with no extra demand on the Hollandsch Diep and Haringvliet. Score 2: it shapes the island's adaptation through the province, the water board and Rijkswaterstaat; no source read shows the Delta Fund paying for a measure on the island.
attributes.affected: Drought brings freshwater shortages its policy must answer, measured nationally: in the Algemene Rekenkamer's report (2026), the 2018 drought did €450 million to €2.08 billion of economic damage in the Netherlands (Ecorys, 2019), and in the KNMI's scenarios an extremely dry summer of today will be an average summer in the future. The Rekenkamer finds that the Delta Programme for Fresh Water, which IenW's minister coordinates, has no concrete, measurable goal, so whether it is on schedule for 2050 cannot be judged; nearly three quarters of the measures studied ran 2.4 to 3 years late, and the first phase's spending, €512.5 million, came 40% above the €364.7 million estimated; while measures are delayed, the damage of drought persists. In the cabinet's reaction to the Delta Programme 2027, the Netherlands had a considerable water shortage in the summer of 2026, raised on 16 July to drought level 2, an actual water shortage: no social disruption, but damage and hindrance, with several functions and interests under pressure. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects IenW.

attributes.label: Rijkswaterstaat
attributes.interest: A safe, liveable and reachable Netherlands, worked on together with others; in drought, the little fresh water of the large rivers and lakes divided as well as it can among all who use it.
attributes.influence: Manages the main water system for IenW, the large rivers, lakes and seas, the Delta waters outside the island's dikes among them, for national safety and fresh water supply. In drought it judges, as the water board does for its waters, whether water runs short, and divides the fresh water of the Rhine and Meuse through weirs, pumping stations and sluices by the verdringingsreeks. Most of Zeeland lies outside the area it can supply, where users depend on rain and groundwater; the island has no fresh water supplied from outside (the municipality, 2023). A pipeline to the island, which the province had explored (2021), would draw on waters it manages: the Volkerak-Zoommeer, at the Noorder Krammer or the Schelde-Rijnkanaal, or the Haringvliet, the study's most future-proof source. Score 2: it shapes the island's adaptation indirectly, through what a supply route could draw on; none exists.
attributes.affected: Drought and salinisation fall on the main water system it manages: as the summer precipitation deficit grows, the possibility of supplying fresh water through the large rivers shrinks (IPLO, 2025). The Algemene Rekenkamer (2026) expects lower river discharges, above all in summer, more and more often, so shipping suffers drought damage more often, and a growing demand for extra flushing against salinisation; at low water levels ships sail with less load, cargo is spread over more ships and waits at the locks grow longer. When less water is available than is needed, it must divide the little fresh water there is by the verdringingsreeks. The Rekenkamer recommends that IenW's minister commission it explicitly as the executor of the Delta Programme's measures in the main water system. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects Rijkswaterstaat, which supplies no water there.

attributes.label: Delta Climate Center
attributes.interest: Regional transitions towards sustainable, climate-resilient and prosperous deltas, in Zeeland and worldwide, with Zeeland as its living lab.
attributes.influence: A partnership of six knowledge institutes, Scalda, HZ University of Applied Sciences, University College Roosevelt, NIOZ, Utrecht University and Wageningen University & Research, at the Kenniswerf in Vlissingen, which started in mid-2023 with a budget of €88 million from the national government and the province, part of the national compensation package Wind in de Zeilen. Its themes for the Zeeland delta are sustainable food, water safety and water availability, and circularity, with three iconic projects from 2024: Delta Protein, the protein transition, mainly marine; Flexible Deltas, flood-defence landscapes that also offer a future for agriculture, salinisation and freshwater availability among their challenges, with living labs on the Westerschelde, the Oosterschelde (from the second half of 2025) and the coastal zone; and ProceZ. Score 1: no source read shows it working on Schouwen-Duiveland or with the island's farmers.
attributes.affected: In its own words, sea level rise, salinisation and drought are among the consequences of climate change noticeable in delta areas such as Zeeland, and it develops knowledge and innovations to keep them safe and flourishing. In its project Flexible Deltas, salinisation and freshwater availability are among the challenges of flood-defending landscapes, from the forelands to the polders behind the dikes, beside water safety, ecological functions and economic interests, which call for an integrated approach. Measured for Zeeland and the Southwest Delta: no source read shows how salinisation on the island, or its farms' adaptation, affects the DCC.
attributes.ask actors: Delta Climate Center, through DCC: Which Zeeland partners take part in Flexible Deltas' Oosterschelde living lab, and whether the DCC works with the water board, the municipality, ZLTO or the island's farmers.
attributes.no relations: Its own pages (home, About us, Research, Flexible Deltas) and NIOZ's news of its start (2023) name none it holds toward an actor on this map: they name its six founding institutes, and its partners in Zeeland only as government bodies, nature and landscape organisations, businesses, umbrella organisations and local communities; none shows it working on Schouwen-Duiveland or with the island's farmers. The province's funding of it is the province's relation.

attributes.label: Deltares
attributes.interest: Applied research on water and the subsurface, for future, sustainable and safe deltas and a resilient infrastructure.
attributes.influence: An independent knowledge institute for applied research on water and the subsurface, working with governments, companies, knowledge institutions, universities and NGOs in the Netherlands and abroad. On the island it carried out, with KWR, Acacia Water, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality, the Living Lab's project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), paid by the EU's rural development fund, the province and the municipality, whose quickscans gave 13 farmers advice on storing fresh water that fits the farm's soil, groundwater and economics, followed by five feasibility studies for groups of farms; drainage and infiltration, it concludes, can store far more fresh water underground than was thought; it wrote the project's final report for the municipality with KWR, Acacia Water and Buro Waterfront. With Acacia Water, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality it had anti-salinisation and double drainage on the low-lying poelgronden of three farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor, demonstrated and monitored (drains laid in 2022, closing meeting in 2024), half paid by the EU; with KWR and WUR it carried out LN2050, research on a climate- and water-robust layout of the countryside towards 2050, the island one of its three example areas, for its farmers, ZLTO's island branch and the Zeeland governments, part of the Ministry of Economic Affairs' Knowledge and Innovation Agenda; in 2025 it was among the knowledge institutes carrying out the national knowledge programme on salt. Score 3: the project's advice reached the participating farms directly; no source read says which partner wrote which advice.
attributes.affected: Salinisation raises knowledge questions it is among those answering: in 2025 it was among the knowledge institutes carrying out the national programme on dealing with salt in agriculture, nature and water management, which LVVN, IenW and STOWA had drawn up because the growing salinisation of water and soil, partly through climate change, raises such questions, to fill fundamental gaps in knowledge, how salty the soil moisture becomes and how salt-tolerant crops are under Dutch conditions, and to make the answers usable in practice in models and tools; €400,000 was available for 2025, and the partners intend to find about €1 million a year for the whole multi-year programme (IPLO, 2025). On the island, the report it wrote with KWR and Acacia Water (Kaandorp et al., 2022) finds the farms' hesitation to invest working both ways: as long as the measures' costs, risks and gain in yield stay uncertain, farmers do not invest, and as long as they do not invest, the techniques are not refined, nothing is learned from building them, their effects cannot be monitored, and no knowledge base forms at agricultural advisory firms and contractors with which the cost of advice and building could fall; it recommends pilots with monitoring, and more research on the measures' economic feasibility. Following the report, it took part in drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). The EU paid half of their cost and the province and the municipality a large part, beside an own contribution from the participating knowledge parties.

attributes.label: KWR
attributes.interest: Knowledge that lets the water sector operate water-wise in an urbanised society, bridging science and practice.
attributes.influence: A knowledge institute of about 210 people, owned by the Dutch water companies, its shareholders since 2006, and Belgium's De Watergroep since 2016; its customers include water companies, water boards, governments, industry and small and medium-sized businesses. On the island it carried out, with Deltares, Acacia Water, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality, the Living Lab's project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), paid by the EU's rural development fund, the province and the municipality, whose quickscans gave 13 farmers advice on storing fresh water that fits the farm's soil, groundwater and economics, followed by five feasibility studies for groups of farms; drainage and infiltration, it concludes, can store far more fresh water underground than was thought, and co-wrote its final report for the municipality; with Deltares and WUR it carried out LN2050, research on a climate- and water-robust layout of the countryside towards 2050, the island one of its three example areas, for its farmers, ZLTO's island branch and the Zeeland governments, part of the Ministry of Economic Affairs' Knowledge and Innovation Agenda; in 2025 it was among the knowledge institutes carrying out the national knowledge programme on salt. Score 3: the project's advice reached the participating farms directly; no source read says which partner wrote which advice.
attributes.affected: In its own words, climate change brings longer periods of drought, more extreme rainfall and less reliable traditional sources of fresh water, while the demand for water grows from drinking water supply, agriculture, industry, nature and cities; it researches the processes behind evaporation and groundwater recharge, and develops solutions such as underground water storage, controlled drainage and subirrigation. Salinisation raises knowledge questions it is among those answering: in 2025 it was among the knowledge institutes carrying out the national programme on dealing with salt in agriculture, nature and water management, which LVVN, IenW and STOWA had drawn up because the growing salinisation of water and soil, partly through climate change, raises such questions, to fill fundamental gaps in knowledge, how salty the soil moisture becomes and how salt-tolerant crops are under Dutch conditions, and to make the answers usable in practice in models and tools; €400,000 was available for 2025, and the partners intend to find about €1 million a year for the whole multi-year programme (IPLO, 2025). On the island, the report it wrote with Deltares and Acacia Water (Kaandorp et al., 2022) finds the farms' hesitation to invest working both ways: as long as the measures' costs, risks and gain in yield stay uncertain, farmers do not invest, and as long as they do not invest, the techniques are not refined, nothing is learned from building them, their effects cannot be monitored, and no knowledge base forms at agricultural advisory firms and contractors with which the cost of advice and building could fall; it recommends pilots with monitoring, and more research on the measures' economic feasibility.

attributes.label: Acacia Water
attributes.interest: Access to clean and safe fresh water for everyone.
attributes.influence: An independent water consultancy, based in Gouda, with 41 employees and work in 19 countries, water for agriculture and groundwater development among its expertise. On the island its hydrologists led farmers in measuring the salinity of the ditches round their fields (Natuurlijk Zoet, 2019–2021, set up with Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the water board, the results in the water board's database); it carried out, with Deltares, KWR, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality, the Living Lab's project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), paid by the EU's rural development fund, the province and the municipality, whose quickscans gave 13 farmers advice on storing fresh water that fits the farm's soil, groundwater and economics, followed by five feasibility studies for groups of farms; drainage and infiltration, it concludes, can store far more fresh water underground than was thought, and co-wrote its final report for the municipality; with Deltares, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality it had anti-salinisation and double drainage on the low-lying poelgronden of three farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor, demonstrated and monitored (drains laid in 2022, closing meeting in 2024), half paid by the EU. Score 3: the project's advice reached the participating farms directly; no source read says which partner wrote which advice.
attributes.affected: In its own words, a rising demand for water and climate change threaten the availability of fresh water for communities, farmers and countries. On the island, the report it wrote with Deltares and KWR (Kaandorp et al., 2022) finds the farms' hesitation to invest working both ways: as long as the measures' costs, risks and gain in yield stay uncertain, farmers do not invest, and as long as they do not invest, the techniques are not refined, nothing is learned from building them, their effects cannot be monitored, and no knowledge base forms at agricultural advisory firms and contractors with which the cost of advice and building could fall; it recommends pilots with monitoring, and more research on the measures' economic feasibility. Following the report, it took part in drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). The EU paid half of their cost and the province and the municipality a large part, beside an own contribution from the participating knowledge parties.

attributes.label: Delphy
attributes.interest: Healthy, successful and sustainable cultivation: better performance for growers, through research, data-driven crop management, advice and training.
attributes.influence: A knowledge company, part of Peterson Solutions, with more than 250 professionals active in over 60 countries and its address in Wageningen; its crop experts advise growers in every plant sector, arable farming among them. It is among the Living Lab's partners, its manager for arable farming and field vegetables in the south-west and two soil and water experts among the partners, and with Acacia Water, Deltares, the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality it had anti-salinisation and double drainage on the low-lying poelgronden of three farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor, demonstrated and monitored (drains laid in 2022, closing meeting in 2024), half paid by the EU. In 2023 it carried out the study of the island's freshwater demand, commissioned and paid for by ZLTO's island branch, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland, with funding from the municipality and the Zuidwestelijke Delta: farming on the island becomes impossible without more fresh water, since the current freshwater measures and innovations supply too little, fit only part of the island, are costly and have not yet proven their value, so a supply of fresh water stays needed and more rain must be stored; ZLTO's island branch draws from it that a supply of fresh water is unavoidable. Score 2: the demonstrations give data on the techniques' effects, and its study informs the island's debate on fresh water; no source read shows it advising individual farms.
attributes.affected: It took part in drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). The EU paid half of their cost and the province and the municipality a large part, beside an own contribution from the participating knowledge parties. No source read shows how salinisation on the island, or its farms' adaptation, affects Delphy otherwise.

attributes.description: Summers with less rain and more evaporation lower the year's rain surplus, which is what recharges the lens. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation: in the year it used, summer evaporation (440 mm) outweighed summer rain (425 mm), so the winter did the recharging, and a smaller surplus gave a thinner lens (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3671, 3674). Within the year.
attributes.sources: de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011

attributes.description: A higher sea raises the water pressure in the sand below the clay, so more salt groundwater seeps up and the ditches get saltier; in the fields the drains will probably catch most of the effect (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 11, for Schouwen-Duiveland). The rise in pressure fades quickly with distance from the coast (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674): in a model of the western Netherlands around Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Utrecht, it reached up to 10 km from the coast and the main rivers, and 5 km inland it was about 40% of the rise (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 3, 9). How much of the rise reaches the dikes along the Grevelingen, which has no tide, the sources read do not say. Within the year: the seepage follows the water pressures, which change constantly (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

attributes.description: More winter rain raises the winter's rain surplus, which recharges the lens. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation, and from October to March of the year it used 397 mm of rain fell against 108 mm of evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665). Kaandorp et al. (2022, p. 11) expect the changing rain to raise the island's winter groundwater levels in part. Within the year.

attributes.description: Rainwater infiltration builds up the floating freshwater lens, but slowly: the lens is a stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673). So a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens. The drains cap how much of a wetter winter reaches the lens: model calculations show that the extra winter water of wetter winters leaves through the intensive tile drainage and does not feed the lens, while higher summer evaporation shrinks it (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12, in an article on the island's seepage fields, by researchers who then present Drains2buffer, a drainage design developed in the GO-FRESH project, as a way to grow the lens).

attributes.description: Where the lens is thin, saline groundwater lies just below the roots and reaches the root zone by capillary rise. In the island's low polders with saline seepage the lens is about 2 m thick, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and capillary rise of saline groundwater is very likely now, possibly damaging crops (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3660, 3662, 3667, 3673, 3675, measured on Schouwen-Duiveland); the topsoil there is fresh thanks to the rainwater lens, which makes farming possible, and these low polders of heavy clay make up a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 10). On Duiveland the salt water reaches into or almost into the root zone in places (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 26). Within the year: in a dry season, with the groundwater below the drains, the flow there is only upward (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

attributes.description: The thinner the lens under the well, the sooner the salt below reaches it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the pumped water grew saltier late in each pumping season, which the report explains by the lens thinning as fresh water is pumped, so that upconing could reach the shallow well (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). Zeeland allows wells only where the fresh groundwater is more than 15 m thick (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). Measured on a creek ridge elsewhere in Zeeland, a lens like those under the island's creek ridges (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year.

attributes.description: Holds in the low polders, where the thin rainwater lens keeps the topsoil fresh, which makes farming possible there (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10, for the island): water anti-salinisation drainage keeps in the lens reaches only the crop on that field, as groundwater and soil moisture, and is expected to lie too deep for its roots at germination (p. 33), when drought mostly falls for the farmers of the low polders (pp. 27, 31); later in the summer the soil supplies a well-established crop (p. 27). The same report rates the crop's use of that water as possibly low in efficiency, as part of it can flow away, and as not steerable, since it sits in the field (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 33, from feasibility studies of five farm clusters in the low polders). In Zeeland fresh groundwater may as a rule be pumped only through horizontal wells, from a fresh body over 15 m thick outside vulnerable areas (p. 26), and on the creek ridges some farmers take water from the ridge through a deep drain (p. 38), one farm using two to irrigate in summer (p. 40), which is Groundwater extraction for irrigation → Freshwater availability for crops. Within the season.

attributes.description: Peat oxidation and clay settling lower the land surface relative to NAP at millimetres a year, so a decimetre takes decades: Dutch land below sea level is still subsiding up to 1 m per century, fastest in peat areas (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 1, 3, 8–9). A rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders is not yet sourced.

attributes.description: The lower a polder lies, the more salt groundwater seeps up into it: on the island the eastern polders lie somewhat higher than the western ones and so have no or far less seepage pressure (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 28), and comparing the island's elevation with a regional groundwater model, seepage occurs in the polders below sea level and rain soaks in on the dunes, the creek ridges and the polders above it, the two strongly correlated (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661, 3673). The optimal drainage depth is the difference between the surface and the ditch level (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 40), so at the same depth a lower polder has a lower ditch level, and a lower level lowers the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater (p. 37). Within the year: the seepage follows the water pressures (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

attributes.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium (Na+) on the clay in place of calcium (Ca2+); once fresh water washes the salt out, clay that holds much sodium disperses: its aggregates and pores collapse, with troubles to be expected above 1 m.e. of exchangeable sodium per 100 g of dry soil. The delay is on the way back: structure begins to decline in the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year in the top 10 cm of soil with calcium carbonate, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on very light soil, while soil without it is expected to recover more slowly (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 225–228, after the 1944–45 inundations in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster, and no source read shows how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay. The only island measurements found lie below the plough layer, to which the loss of crumb structure is confined (van Beekom et al., 1953b, p. 226): on a tile-drained agricultural field with permanent saline seepage, sodium made up 9% of the exchangeable cations at 1.6 m between drains and 3% at 3 m near a drain, well below a flooded soil's 21%, the 9% above and the 3% below the roughly 5% at which structure may suffer (Eeman et al., 2017, pp. 225–227, 238–239; van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 225–226). A national knowledge agenda judges, from experience within the SALTA knowledge cluster, that salinisation seems so far to cause little damage to soil structure in the Netherlands, where elevated SAR, ESP or CROSS values are usually not determined (Knol et al., 2025, p. 43).
attributes.simplification: Folds Sodium on the clay, a stock between the two: the salt puts sodium on the clay, and the sodium breaks the clay's structure once the salt washes out. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes, and the stock's slowness is the link's delay. What one link distorts: the delay lies on the way back only, the structure beginning to decline in the first winter after the salt leaches out and recovering over years, while the link draws one delay for both ways.

attributes.description: Upward saline seepage keeps the rainwater lens thin. On the island the lens in the seepage areas is mostly under 2 m (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10), on average 2 m in a helicopter survey of its low polders, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and it thickens sharply where the flow turns from seepage to infiltration (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3660, 3673, 3675, measured on the island, the fluxes from the regional groundwater model). That a larger seepage flux gives a thinner lens comes from a model of a tile-drained field built from the island's field data (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3671, 3674). In that model the centre of the mixing zone at a drain always stays within 0.1 m of the drain depth, so seepage moves the lens between the drains, and recharge and drainage depth control it alongside seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3659, 3671, 3673–3674); in the model a poorly permeable layer below the drains thins the lens between them and one above them thickens it (p. 3674), and unripened clay, a poorly permeable layer, lies close to the surface over a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 32, 55). A delay, its length open: in that model, started fully saline, 30 years of simulation sufficed for every run to become stationary (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665), an upper bound; no source read gives how fast the lens follows a change in seepage.

attributes.description: Rain recharges the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, pp. 230, 233, 236, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Even so, in most of the well-drained soils at least 150 mm still seeped through in winter, and less in badly drained soils of low permeability, against a Dutch annual rain surplus of about 200 mm, most of it in winter (van Beekom et al., 1953a, pp. 155, 157). In model computations of wetter winters, the extra winter water drained off effectively through the intensive drainage without feeding the thin rain lenses of the saline seepage areas the authors studied in Zeeland, among them a tile-drained field on the island, so more rain soaking in may add little to the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, pp. 6, 11, 12, by authors who report on the GO-FRESH project, which developed a drainage system to grow the lens). Within the year: the structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in. How thick a lens the recharge builds is also set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674).

attributes.description: A seedbed in soil with its structure lets the crops germinate better, with less resowing, and yields rise, most for crops sensitive to structure: on flooded clay in Zeeland, plots whose structure gypsum restored yielded up to 15% more sugar beet, 8% more onions and, on heavy clay, up to twice the summer barley, while cereals on light soil gained little (van Beekom et al., 1953b, p. 234, Table 9). Part of the gain is the longer time to work the soil, the link through Spring workability of the fields. Within the year.

attributes.description: Fresh water supplied from outside adds to what crops can draw on: the island's farming depends on the rain that falls and is stored in the root zone or underground, and none is brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 4), which leaves farms short of water in dry periods (p. 8). How much of a supply reaches crops depends on how it is spread: in a design estimate by an engineering consultancy for Provincie Zeeland, a supply through the island's ditches needs 5 m3/s, of which about 2.8 m3/s is pumped back out at the drainage pumping stations (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 40), and it picks up salt from saline seepage on the way (p. 45), to an estimated average of 500 to 800 mg Cl/l at sprinkling against 95 to 500 mg Cl/l at the three sources considered (p. 42), figures the study calls only a very rough indication (pp. 40, 43), above the 300 mg Cl/l damage threshold of salt-sensitive crops (p. 45). A ring pipeline needs 2 m3/s and sprinkles at the source's quality (pp. 42, 45). Within the season.

attributes.description: Active infiltration adds winter water to the lens, on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay: the creek-ridge infiltration system raises the groundwater through the drains in winter so the lens grows, and the Freshmaker and underground storage inject winter water through a deep drain or a well, all to pump in summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–22, 38, for the island). What limits it on most of the island is fresh water to infiltrate, since the surface water is mostly saline and drain water the likeliest source (pp. 38, 43, 55), and the permit (pp. 26, 45). Years to a decade, so a delay: on the island's own creek ridge, infiltration with controlled drainage added about 60,000 m³ of fresh water under a 9.5-ha field in ten years and thickened the lens by up to 3.5 m (p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050); under a creek ridge on Walcheren, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, pp. 1424–1425, 1429, a model result, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

attributes.description: Measures in the low polders keep rain in the field instead of draining it off: controlled drainage and anti-salinisation drainage raise the drains' outflow level, so more water stays in the ground of the field (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 17–18, 29, for the island). On the island's trials raising the drains' outflow level did not plainly keep the water in the field: at Kerkwerve raising the control well barely raised the existing drains' level on one strip, so their discharge fell only very slightly (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 91), and near Dreischor, where on one of the two anti-salinisation plots the groundwater never rose to the raised outflow level and the drains did not flow, the authors suspect the groundwater flows away elsewhere (van Hateren et al., 2025, p. 58). Double drainage catches rain rather than keeping it in the field: on two pilots near Kerkwerve its shallow drains carried off 43 to 52% of the winter's net rain to be caught, with little influence on groundwater levels (van Hateren et al., 2025, pp. 4, 77). Within the year.

attributes.description: What farmers pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens, the boundary with the saline groundwater below rising: the water board's limit of 800 m³ per hectare a year rests on the balance between recharge by rain, irrigation water and extraction, set to keep the fresh groundwater in stock and the fresh-salt boundary from rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b), and pumping too fast risks salinisation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within those rules the effects are meant to stay within the farm's field, with in principle no depletion, and Deltares's modelling of the rules (2018) found that in general they seem enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around the well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland). How fast the lens responds to pumping, no source read shows. In one pilot at Sirjansland, a deep drain pumped about 4,500 m³ a year for two years from a lens thinner than the 15 m the rules require: after the first season the deep monitoring wells showed no salinisation at the bottom or edge of the lens, and after the second geophysical measurements showed the EC at 11 m depth rising, possibly a sign that the pumping shifted the fresh-salt boundary, in data strongly affected by the wet years 2023 and 2024 (Acacia Water, n.d., a consultancy testing with the grower whether small lenses can be managed sustainably, funded by the European Commission and the Province of Zeeland). Its model finds the resistance of any separating layers important for the calculated upconing of saline water, with more to pump where it is higher (Acacia Water, n.d.), and under the creek ridges in the east of the island the deeper subsoil to about 25 m is mostly fine sand with local thin clay layers (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 38).

attributes.description: The more a well pumps from the lens, the further salt groundwater rises towards it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the water pumped from the shallow well grew saltier as each pumping season went on (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). The report on the island's freshwater measures lists salinisation at too high a pumping rate as a risk of the creek-ridge infiltration system and of underground storage (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within the year: the cone follows the season's pumping.

attributes.description: Rain the drains carry off does not refill the lens: tile drains usually discharge shallow groundwater rapidly during rain, as other studies found (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661), and recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness, by measurements on the island and a model built from them (pp. 3662, 3673–3675). In a conceptual 2-D model of a tile-drained field with saline seepage, built from field measurements in Zeeland and a 3-D model of a field on the island, how readily the drains run (a drainage resistance of 0.5 to 7.5 days) changed the lens's depth and width by less than 0.1 m; across the model's parameters the lens's depth moved more between the drains than at them, where the centre of the mixing zone stayed within 0.1 m of drain depth (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3662, 3664–3666, 3671). Within the year.

attributes.description: A larger harvest per hectare raises income at a given price, the price being World prices of conventional crops. The + holds in full where only the island's yield falls, to salt or a local shortage of fresh water. A dry summer across north-west Europe also raises the price, since the harvests there set it: for potatoes, north-west Europe is one market, and their price was highest in the extremely dry 2018 (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). Then what a farm loses depends on how it sells: in 2018, higher prices could help onion growers make up for a harvest forecast 44% below the year before, while potato growers mostly held contracts at prices agreed in advance (NOS, 2018), some 80% of the crop at around nine cents a kilo while free-market potatoes reached 30 (DutchNews.nl, 2018); onions are rarely sold under such contracts (Bogosavac, 2018). On the island, a farm with its own stored water can gain from the high prices of a dry year (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 36). For seed potatoes, 8% of the island's cropping plan in 2021 (Delphy, 2023, p. 42), the price is set mainly by size grade, with the coarse sizes paid much less, so a lack of water at tuber set gives fewer tubers, often made up in kilograms by larger ones that are poorly paid (Delphy, 2023, p. 44, advisers' judgement in a report commissioned by the island's farmers' association). For them the + holds for the kilograms in the best-paid sizes, 28–50 mm, not for weight alone (p. 44). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R8: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.
attributes.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so R8 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

attributes.description: With the same debt, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (p. 21). A high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (p. 19); the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value. It holds for the land a farm owns: farms owning little of it barely gain from a rising price (p. 26). While land rose the ratio moved little: from 2006 to 2015 Dutch arable farms' balance sheet per farm doubled, mainly through the rise in the land price, while their solvency rose only from 76% to 78% and their bank loans went from just over 5,000 to 10,000 euro per ha, an unchanged 16% share (Silvis et al., 2017, p. 2, national farm accounts). The note was commissioned by a.s.r. vastgoed vermogensbeheer (p. 4). Within the year: the farm accounts value the land each year (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13).

attributes.description: For every loan a bank must hold capital, as the law on banks' solvency sets, the more the higher the credit risk, and the cost of that capital, the return its shareholders require, is part of the interest each client pays (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a). The final Basel III standards raise that capital, EU banks' minimum Tier 1 capital requirement by an estimated 9.0% at full implementation in 2028 (European Banking Authority, 2023). Together the two make stricter capital rules raise what a bank charges for a loan. Measured across EU banks: no source read gives the change for Dutch farm loans. Within the year: the bank prices the capital with each loan.

attributes.description: Soil work for potatoes should not be done when the soil is too wet, which can smear and compact it; for onions, too-wet soil work can keep a well-crumbled seedbed from forming, and in March and April, as the scenarios' rain rises, unfavourable conditions for it may become more likely; where blight cannot be well controlled, as in organic farming, a potato crop is best planted early where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, pp. 25, 27, for the Netherlands, from a cultivation guide, a crop study and an expert). So, by inference from that guide, the more of the rotation they take, the more farmers need fields that dry early in spring. Holding water back longer, as a buffer for dry times, is sometimes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44); on Duiveland the board moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the soil work allows (2021a, p. 66). No source read shows how much spring soil work the new crops need: the sign rests on their needing less. Quinoa, a salt-tolerant crop, also needs soil work in spring: in the Netherlands it is sown from the end of March to the end of April and needs a fine seed bed (van Loo, 2023, pp. 75, 77, by a Wageningen breeder whose group develops quinoa varieties), so the sign holds where the share moves to crops sown in autumn or winter, such as winter wheat, sown from mid-September to early February (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 29), less clearly where it moves to quinoa; and on clay and zavel, the main topsoil of the island's western low polders (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27), the main soil work for potatoes is often done before winter (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25). Within the year.

attributes.description: A farm that relies on high margins can give fewer hectares to lower-margin new crops.

More income from the land raises what buyers bid for it, through what they expect an extra hectare to earn an expanding farm over the years of the investment rather than through last year's income (Farjon et al., 2013, box Maximale biedprijs; Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 2–3). The + holds beside drivers the island's farms cannot move: since 1970 the nominal Dutch price has risen more than tenfold while net value added rose two- to threefold, carried by scale enlargement and falling interest rates (Farjon et al., 2013, introduction and section Ontwikkeling van de prijs). Across individual land transactions in the Netherlands from 2004 to 2011, the expected revenue from the land had a significant positive effect on the price, beside land regulations, the spatial environment and local market conditions (Boere, 2015, pp. 81, 98). Years: its swings ran over years, the real price rising sharply and then falling by half in the late 1970s and by 30% between 1995 and 2005 (Farjon et al., 2013, section Ontwikkeling van de prijs): a delay.

attributes.description: More income leaves more, after the household's spending and the farm's payment obligations, repayments included, to save for investment; a negative income leaves too little to reserve, and machines then age (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25). A farm with good solvency can probably take up extra credit when its income is negative, the same report judges, and Dutch arable farms averaged close to 80% solvency in 2015, land more than two thirds of their balance sheet (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25; national farm accounts, no figure for the island), so a poor year may shrink what a solvent farm can invest less than its income. A lasting low income is harder to bridge: the bank looks hard at long-term continuity before deferring payments or giving extra credit (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28), and in a simulation of banks' credit checks, which base a new loan on the past three years' net cash flow, solvency was the limit in only 1.2% of farm observations and net cash flow in almost all cases (Lamkowsky, 2023, pp. 51–52, 56, 101; Dutch dairy farms, 2009–2017). Within the year: income adds to the savings in the year it is earned.

attributes.description: Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for a storage measure, not whether it wants to.

Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for the switch (new machines, the first years of a new crop), not whether it wants to. The costs of salt-tolerant seed and soil amendments may not make up for the yield and income salt takes in the first years, when setting up costs most, and the benefits are not always obvious in the short term (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 60); farms whose financial buffers shrank in the corona crisis were expected to be less willing to invest, slowing their modernisation and sustainability, and banks often count financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven as a risk (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 6). For samphire and sea aster the outlet, not only capacity to invest, limits adoption: their food market is small and easily saturated, in the authors' judgement (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), and growers in Zeeland's saline cultivation, eight in all, say there is little room for new entrants, and that making room would also take strong growth of the market for saline vegetables (Delphy, 2023, p. 49, a consultancy report commissioned by Agrarisch Schouwen Duiveland that argues for a freshwater supply, p. 50). Delphy adds that cheaper imports compete and that few of Zeeland's soils suit these crops, but sees openings in high-end restaurants and retail if the season can be lengthened, and in other saline crops less grown abroad (p. 49). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Higher temperatures and drier weather raise evapotranspiration, the water crops use when they have enough, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56). Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.
attributes.simplification: Folds Crop water demand, a step between the two with no actor and no decision: hotter, drier summers raise what crops need, and what they need beyond the water they get is the shortfall. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: what crops need is no variable of its own, so a crop's own water need, new crops against the current ones, cannot enter; no source read shows whether the new crops need less.

attributes.description: Rain, irrigation and capillary rise from the groundwater add water to the root zone and lower its depletion; once the depletion passes the readily available water, the crop uses less water than it needs (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eqs. 84–85, a daily water balance). So the more fresh water crops can draw on, the smaller the shortfall, within the season. On the island's farms a gift of 20 to 25 mm at germination can make the difference where none can be given now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 55). In the low western polders (Scharendijke–Brouwershaven–Kerkwerve) the farmers in the project's quickscans find drought a problem mainly at germination: once the crop has come up well, the soil's good moisture supply keeps drought damage later in summer limited even in dry years, and waterlogging is often felt as the larger problem (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27), though a study paid for by the island's farmers' association assumes a much larger water need (Delphy, 2023, p. 40). How much extra water eases also depends on crop and year: raising the water table by subirrigation on a test field at Rusthoeve on Noord-Beveland, on sandy clay (zavel) with saline seepage, raised dry-matter yield against a reference field by 18 % for onions in dry 2022 but by 2 to 7 % for chicory in dry 2020 and for wheat and potato in normal-to-wet 2021 (Terink et al., 2023, p. 44, a trial by KnowH2O and KWR paid for by the province, the water board and the municipality of Noord-Beveland).

attributes.description: Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's). On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the surface water hold high salt levels, and no fresh water can be brought in during dry periods (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). They may pump only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick (p. 26), which lies under the creek ridges and the dunes (p. 10): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not sprinkle, some trying drip irrigation, while on a creek ridge a livestock farmer pumps from two deep drains for grassland in the summer season, more in dry years, and an arable farmer occasionally irrigates about 20 mm at germination, the report not saying where that water comes from (pp. 27–28, 40, 43). So the link runs where a farm has fresh groundwater under it. The rules cap each well's pumping: under Waterschap Scheldestromen's general rule a well may take at most 800 m³ a year per hectare of its parcel (80 mm) and 8,000 m³ a year, a permit with conditions being possible where a well cannot meet them (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 and its explanation). For the creek ridges of the south-western delta, Deltares researchers presenting a system to enlarge their fresh lenses stated in 2015, under the rules of that time, that irrigation demand already exceeded the permissible extraction, which led to crop damage (Pauw et al., 2015, p. 1415, a statement, not a measurement), so in a dry summer a growing shortfall may end in crop damage rather than in more pumping. Within the year.

attributes.description: What farmers pump is fresh water their crops get: what pumping gains them. In the study's options for the island it goes onto the field by reel sprinkler or by drip, and the method influences how much of it the crop gets: drip loses less water, so a cubic metre covers more land, while a reel usually gives several gifts per hectare (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 35, in its cost-benefit analysis for the island's farms). On a cluster of three farms on a creek ridge, a livestock farmer irrigates grassland in dry years, in midsummer too, from two deep drains under a permit of up to 16,000 m³ a year (pp. 40, 43). Across the whole island it is a small flow: a water balance from model output and the water board's permits puts groundwater irrigation at 0.33 million m³ a summer half-year, taken at the permitted maximum since what is actually pumped is unknown, against a precipitation deficit of about 30 million m³ in the dry summer of 2018 (Krajenbrink et al., 2023, pp. 44, 46, 48; the authors call the irrigation figures probably inaccurate and the groundwater irrigation of 2018 still on the low side, pp. 45, 47). Of what a reel sprays, about 60% went to crop growth on potatoes and onions, against 80 to 90% for drip on onions, measured at Philippine in Zeeuws-Vlaanderen with the farmer sprinkling in the evening and not in wind, in a project with an irrigation firm in its team (Acacia Water, 2020, pp. ii, 7, 25). The salt a well may draw up with the water runs through Upconing of salt groundwater. Within the season: within the year, no delay.

attributes.description: A crop that uses less water than it needs yields less, in proportion: its relative yield falls by a crop's yield response factor times its relative shortfall in evapotranspiration, over the season 1.1 for potatoes and onions, 1.0 for sugar beet and 1.05 for winter wheat, the loss small in the vegetative and ripening periods and large in flowering and yield formation (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eq. 90 and Table 24, after FAO paper 33, general). On the island, farmers in the western low polders find the shortfall falls mostly at germination, and a crop that emerged well loses little to drought later in the summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27); a potato grower at Nieuwerkerk lost a fifth of his 2026 harvest, the potatoes smaller too, when growth stopped in the June heat and the rain came too late, the water in many of Zeeland's ditches too saline to irrigate from and the region short of fresh water (van Essen, 2026). In a water-need study for the island paid for by the farmers' association Agrarisch Schouwen Duiveland, Delphy's south-west arable advisers count only a quarter of the season's shortfall towards the water need of sugar beet and winter wheat, whose long growing season lets them make up a shortfall later with strong growth, and half for grass seed and ware potatoes, mostly late ones, which compensate somewhat less, late ware potatoes still giving reasonable yields in dry years through rain late in the season (Delphy, 2023, pp. 1, 32). These factors come from Delphy's experience in practice, and Delphy calls the result still fairly optimistic, since drought may also fall at other moments, later in the summer or at tuber set (Delphy, 2023, p. 33). Within the season.

attributes.description: A supply route carries fresh water to the island: since the island is not connected to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought to it in dry periods (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). What a route delivers depends on its source: two of the three sources explored lie in the Volkerak-Zoommeer, the third is the Haringvliet (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 7, for Provincie Zeeland), and algae stop the inlets from that lake, on Tholen in seven of the years 2003–2011 and on average from 20 July, and, as algae growth declines, at the factsheet's writing (2013) only from about mid-August (Schipper et al., 2014, p. 36, a factsheet for Tholen), and in July 2026 rising blue-green algae there led Waterschap Brabantse Delta to ban taking surface water in two polders, the Prins Hendrikpolder and the Auvergnepolder, fed from the lake, through the Schelde-Rijnkanaal among others, which have no other supply route (Waterschap Brabantse Delta, 2026, p. 1). Within the year, once a route exists.

attributes.description: Dry summers lower the discharge of the great rivers, and drought more often brings a water shortage, in which the scarce water is divided among drinking water, nature, agriculture and shipping (KNMI, 2023, p. 42, the Planbureau voor de Leefomgeving's risks for the Netherlands, measured nationally): a route can only carry what summer discharge and the national distribution in drought (the verdringingsreeks, IenW and Rijkswaterstaat) leave for the region, outside the CLD's scale. Within the year: a summer's discharge sets that summer's supply.
attributes.simplification: Folds Fresh water available for supply in drought: dry summers leave less river water for a supply route, and the route carries what is left. The sign is the product of the two steps (−, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: the river water left for the region in drought, which the national distribution decides outside the CLD's scale, is no variable of its own.

attributes.description: The body deciding on a route weighs the call; so far a study has followed and no route has been decided on (Freshwater supply route to the island). Years, so a delay: a route has to be decided on and paid for, and implementing its pipeline alone is expected to take about 3 to 10 years (Freshwater supply route to the island).

Clay that has lost its structure stays wet long into spring, so it can be worked only late and the time to make a seedbed is very short; restored with gypsum, it dries sooner and can be worked for a longer period (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 233–234, on clay in Zeeland flooded by the sea in 1944–45, the sodium breaking down the structure as in Clay dispersion & sodification). attributes.description: The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the sooner the fields drain and dry after rain. By the water board's rules for its whole area, the drooglegging is set at an optimum for each use and soil, against both wet and drought damage (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 7); at half the design discharge it must keep a field's drains, laid at their optimal depth, all but above the ditch water (p. 8); and an area 10 cm or more short of its optimum counts as too wet (p. 9). Once the drooglegging reaches that optimum the drains already lie clear of the ditch water by the rule above, so a deeper level should, by inference, add little workability; on Duiveland the board's model test finds the drooglegging more than 40 cm past its optimum (60 cm on schorgronden) in large parts of the area in all situations, against 10 of 31 level areas with more than 10% of their surface too wet in a normal winter and 11 in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 32, 42). On the Rusthoeve trial farm, measured on Noord-Beveland on zavel with saline seepage and an average drooglegging of 1.6 m, a drain outlet held 30 cm higher raised the groundwater on average 10 cm near the ditch and 20 cm mid-field with no adverse effect on workability, by the farm's experience, on blocks redrained at 6 m instead of about 12 m (Schipper et al., 2015, pp. 6, 15, 17–18, 76; funded by the Province of Zeeland, ZLTO and the water board, along with national and Interreg funds, p. 11). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40), and the move from the winter to the summer level in spring follows the farmers' soil work (p. 66). Within the season, no delay.

attributes.description: Fields that cannot be worked in time are planted late: a later planting date can shorten the potato's growing season, since later in the season it is often too wet to harvest, and where blight cannot be controlled, as in organic farming, it costs yield, so an early date is preferred where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, from a crop study and an expert, for the Netherlands). attributes.description: Where fields stay too wet to work, farmers want lower ditch levels: what deep drainage gains them. In the water board's words, holding water back longer as a buffer for dry times is sometimes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44, its management programme for its whole area): the board's account of the farmers' interest, not the farmers' own. No source read shows how much a wet spring raises the demand. The water board's own model test of the current levels, which compares computed ditch levels with the optimum drainage depth for each soil and use and does not measure workability, finds more than 10% of the surface too wet in a normal winter in 9 of the 43 level areas outside nature in Schouwen's polder, but 18 under the summer level, 62% of the area, which the board brings in step by step in March–April (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 19, 32–36, 43–44, 56); on Duiveland 10 of 31 tested areas are more than 10% too wet in a normal winter and 11 in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 42). The link so seems to act mainly around that switch and in the wetter areas. Within the year.

attributes.description: The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the more peat lies above the groundwater, where it compacts and oxidises, so the land falls faster: by the water board's rules for its whole area, peat soil above the groundwater subsides in response to drainage, and where the soil is prone to settling the board changes levels with restraint to limit it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 13). On the island it holds Schouwen's summer levels high on purpose to limit subsidence by peat compaction, which leaves the salt-marsh soils between too little drainage depth (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 45), and changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (p. 50); Duiveland's plan changed levels with great care where peat lies below (2021a, p. 67). Within the year: the board weighs the risk by the summer groundwater level against the ditch level and the depth of the peat (2021b, p. 50). No source read gives how much faster the land falls per decimetre of drainage.

attributes.description: Lower ditch levels lower the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater, so the seepage pressure rises; a higher level lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, the board's analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). The seepage is driven by the higher water pressure at greater depth, in the first aquifer below the polders' clay (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 10–11, 28). A raise in one level area can also lift the head in the shared first aquifer around it, so seepage can rise on the land next to it: in a model of a 110 km2 low-lying polder inundated in 2100, seepage in the polder fell but rose in the adjacent areas, a net cut of only 9% of the polder's salt load (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 8–9, 13–14, modelled in the western Netherlands). On Schouwen's south coast a seepage ditch rings the raised nature area so that its higher level does not add seepage on the land around it (van Haperen et al., 2006, p. 3, Staatsbosbeheer, which manages part of the area, an account without data). Within the year: the water pressures in the top layer change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

attributes.description: The board holds the ditch levels lower in winter than in summer to prevent water damage in winter, and a higher winter level would keep the groundwater from sinking as deep (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, its analysis for Duiveland): the deeper the ditches stand in winter, the more of the rain they and the drains carry off. On a creek ridge studied for water storage, where the winter depth is over 1.5 m in large parts, the drains and ditches carry the excess rain off fast, and a higher winter level might raise the groundwater and with it the recharge (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 42–43). Within the year.

attributes.description: A water level plan sets the levels the board pursues and maintains in normal circumstances (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021d, 2022), after its procedure: the executive board adopts a draft, open to views for six weeks; the general board adopts the plan; appeal is open for six weeks (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18), for Duiveland from February to August 2021 (2021a, p. 53; 2021d). Its levels take effect on a date the plan sets, which depends partly on the works they need (2025, p. 18): Duiveland's plan proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, most possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged (2021a, p. 69), and the works for that were still being put to the island in March 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026a). In summer the levels a plan sets may not hold: the board's own study for Duiveland says that in many areas, where the winter level is low and the summer level set well above it, the higher summer level can usually be held for a few weeks and then sinks slowly into the soil, depending on location and soil, and that without water supply, which the island lacks (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8), the summer level may not be maintainable in a rainfall deficit (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 66). Years, so a delay.

attributes.description: The water board weighs farmers' need for low levels against raising them: it involves farming among the interest groups as it prepares a plan and weighs their input (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17), and on Duiveland moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the farmers' soil work allows (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 66). How much the farmers' views weigh against the board's other aims, no source read shows: on Duiveland four views against a raise the plan proposed to study did not change the plan (p. 53). The board's guideline tests a level area against a norm: the norm for farmland derives from the optimal drain depths for farming (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 7); with more than 10% of the area too wet the level must be lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved, with less a raise is considered (p. 9). On Duiveland, by the board's research report for its plan of 2021, a level change in most level areas is possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged (2021a, p. 69). Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years, weighing among other things the reports of those concerned, finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: The water board names the gradually increasing salinisation a concern for the fresh water farming needs, the thin fresh groundwater lenses most threatened, and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses: by not lowering target levels much, since a lower level lowers the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater and raises the seepage pressure, while a raise lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, a criterion of its analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). So the more seepage salts the soil's fresh water, the more reason the board has to raise levels, the lens being what it protects (Saline seepage → Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (p. 69); how far seepage weighed there against drought, no source read shows. Elsewhere on the island the board gives drought as its reason: on Schouwen, where nearly the whole polder gets seepage, it raises the level in ten level areas to limit drought damage, with larger fresh water stocks in the soil as the effect, its method naming seepage only as a ground to deviate from the guideline that 10% of a level area may be too wet (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 26, 36–37, 53), and its framework for every level plan from 2025 names neither seepage nor the lenses among its criteria for a raise (2025, pp. 9, 12). So the board's accounts read give the link little support on the island: in them, the Duiveland criterion above is the only stated reason for a raise that names the lenses. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17).
