attributes.description: Rising pumping costs give the water board a reason to raise the levels.

By the water board's rules, the views sent on a draft plan within six weeks are answered in the decision, anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it, and the board consults the region first so that as few conflicts as possible arise to slow or interrupt the procedure (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). So objections can delay, change or stop a plan to raise the levels while it is pending; with none pending they change nothing, and they never lower a level. On the island the views on the two plans of 2021 changed neither: Duiveland's 25 views from six people (2021a, p. 53) and Schouwen's 11 from five, which added some studies (2021b, pp. 7–8). As the board summarises the views, four on Duiveland's proposed study of a raise gave as their concern that flooding becomes likelier in extreme rain, not the land's value (2021a, p. 53), and its summary of Schouwen's names none against the raises in its ten level areas (2021b, pp. 7–8, 53). The region's reactions before each draft were taken into the work on it (2021a, pp. 52–53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether anyone appealed either plan, no source read shows. Elsewhere in Zeeland a view did change the same board's plan: on the raise of a winter level in the Braakman, near Terneuzen, ZLTO objected for seven farmers that one party's gain should not harm another, and the plan of 2015 took a phased raise, its first step only once the field that suffers most has been acquired and its second within six years (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). By the board's own rules, damage from a deliberate change of a field's drainage depth that is significant, disproportionate and beyond normal social risk is likely to be compensated, where possible by technical measures or by buying or exchanging land and, failing agreement, by a claim decided apart from the plan with its own objection and appeal (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 14–15, 18); in the Braakman an independent valuer was to assess the expected damage on the field that may suffer disproportionately (2015, p. 2). So where an owner's loss passes that threshold, an objection over it may be answered without dropping the raise, though no source read shows how often that happens. Within the year, as the plan is decided.

attributes.description: Seepage that reaches the ditches is pumped out with the rain: across most of Duiveland the waterways catch salt or brackish seepage from below (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 20); Schouwen's water comes mainly from rain and partly from seepage, strongest at its edges and in the low inlagen (2021b, pp. 25–26), all of it flowing to the pumping stations (2021b, p. 24), as Duiveland's whole area is drained by pumping (2021a, p. 21); and the low western polders, under seepage, drain their brackish to salt water through pumping stations (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The board's electricity cost moves with the water it pumps: in the dry year 2025 its water systems spent €1.1 million less on electricity than budgeted, for the drought, and extreme rain can raise the electricity cost of its sewage and polder pumping stations by up to 25% (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026e, pp. 18, 55); seepage is part of the water pumped, so more seepage costs more, within the year, though the source does not name seepage. No source read gives seepage's share of the water pumped on the island.

attributes.description: The board passes its pumping costs on through its levy, part of the costs of its water management, of which unbuilt land other than nature carries 22.78% for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026c, art. 2). One rate holds across its whole area, so a cost that rises on the island is spread over all of it: the law lets the board charge pumped areas up to 100% more (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 122), and its ordinance for 2026 does not.

attributes.description: The levy is a cost to the farm that holds the land: the law charges those who hold unbuilt land by ownership, possession or a limited right, not its tenants (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 117), at one rate per hectare (art. 121), €115.53 for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026d, art. 6), and a farm's income is its revenue minus the costs it pays and depreciation (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21). Whether a tenant pays it through the rent, no source read shows. Within the year: the levy is charged each year.

attributes.description: Once a crop's root zone salinity, as the conductivity of the saturated soil extract (ECe), passes its threshold, its yield falls in proportion to the excess (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 89): onions lose 16% per dS/m above 1.2 dS/m and potatoes 12% above 1.7, rated sensitive and moderately sensitive, against 5.9% above 7.0 for sugar beet and 7.1% above 6.0 for wheat (Table 23), so on the island's rotations salt takes most from potatoes and onions. The harm is osmotic at once and comes from sodium or chloride building up in the leaves more slowly (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656). Table 23 is a guideline from experiments mostly under irrigation, the soil kept close to field capacity (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8), tolerance varying with climate, soil and practice, and crops often less tolerant as they germinate and as seedlings (Table 23, note 1): crop physiology that, by inference, holds on the island's fields too, its thresholds not measured there. Field trials at Salt Farm Texel, on sand irrigated with saline water, find gentler lines for potatoes and onions: across 13 potato cultivars a threshold of 3.2 dS/m and a slope of 6.1% per dS/m on average over the cultivars and years (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 1, 5), and for onions thresholds of 2.4–5.9 dS/m and slopes of 7.4–11.7% per dS/m, with wide confidence intervals (de Vos et al., 2016, p. 22); both come from the trial farm's own trials, written by its staff with university co-authors, the 2021 one partly funded by the Salt Farm Foundation, and may not hold on clay (de Vos et al., 2016, pp. 2, 9; van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 1, 11). A review for the Deltaprogramma Zoetwater judges that the rule over- or underestimates the loss, not reproducibly, where root-zone salinity varies within the season, as it mostly does in Dutch open-field farming (van Bakel et al., 2018, pp. 30–31): on the island the sign holds, but these lines do not fix the size of the loss. Within the season.

attributes.description: Harvest lost to salt is income lost: at the farm, salt lowers the yield and raises the cost of inputs such as fresh water and soil amendments (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). For potatoes north-west Europe should be seen as one market, the size of its harvest showing in the price (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8), so salt on the island's fields alone does not move it, and a harvest lost to salt is lost at that price. Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: A field moved from a current crop to a new salt-tolerant one no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take: the link holds by what Harvest lost to salt counts, the fields still under the current crops. The new crops lose less to salt, not nothing: 10 to 19 of the 50 experts and stakeholders interviewed across the Netherlands' salinisation-prone provinces say that, in general, salts affect the soil's structure and so lower yields even where a crop is or becomes more tolerant, and that the salt level at which cultivation on clay stops being effective is largely uncertain (Beauchampet, 2022, pp. 213–214, 221, interviews, not measurements); the island's polders generally have clayey soils (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year, from the next season's crop.
attributes.simplification: The new crops are taken to lose nothing to salt. That comes nearest to true for crops that can be grown on saline land, such as sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat (EU CAP Network, 2023), and for quinoa, among the crops better suited to saline conditions, though how far salt limits a crop depends on the crop (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 63). A new crop as sensitive as the current ones loses about as much, and R6 does not run through it.

attributes.description: A salt-tolerant variety loses less of its harvest at the same salinity of the root zone: in field trials on Texel from 2012 to 2018, most potato cultivars kept 90% of their yield up to a soil salinity (ECe) of about 4 to 5 dS/m, some about twice that (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 1–2), Elgar and Rivola above 7.5 dS/m (p. 10). Measured on sandy soil, the salt brought by irrigation water: the sign holds on the island, since the trials relate yield to the salinity of the root zone, which drives Harvest lost to salt there whatever brings the salt; the size need not, as the authors warn for other soils and climates (p. 11). Past the salinity at which they keep 90% of their yield, Elgar and Rivola lose yield faster than the other cultivars, in estimates whose large uncertainties, the authors note, make significant differences between cultivars hard to find (van Straten et al., 2021, p. 6); a larger ECe90 goes with a steeper decline, so all cultivars reach about the same lethal soil salinity, 20–24 dS/m (pp. 1, 5), and the advantage narrows as salinity approaches it. The study was partly funded by the Salt Farm Foundation (p. 11).

attributes.description: A hectare moved from a high-margin current crop to a new one earns the new crop's margin instead, and the margin of protein crops cannot compete with most other crops (Polman et al., 2026, p. 9). The link holds by what the element counts, the hectares taken from the high-margin crops: the area of protein crops, rarely a farm's main crop, likely depends on the room left in the rotation (Polman et al., 2026, p. 17), and in a simulation for Flanders quinoa mostly took the place of maize and winter wheat (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 3). On the island without extra fresh water, a scenario calculation for a model 100 ha farm with prices held fixed, in a report commissioned and co-financed by the island's farmers' association Agrarisch Schouwen Duiveland, puts the margin of sown onions in the 2022 crop plan at €1,197 a hectare, at 25 tonnes against 60 with enough fresh water, below grain's €1,348 and far below the €6,635 of potatoes for processing, and expects onions to shrink or leave the island by 2030 (Delphy, 2023, pp. 1, 3, 42–45). A field moved from onions then gives up little, drought losses being counted in the current crop's margin. Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: A tolerant variety earns less than the variety it replaces where salt does not limit the crop: salt-tolerant varieties are usually lower yielding, high-yielding varieties being sensitive to stress through a trade-off between tolerance and yield (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 30). In greenhouse pots at Wageningen in 2024, a salt-tolerant potato variety lost 18% of its tuber weight under salt against 39% for a sensitive one (p. 21), yet on fresh water it netted about €1,800 a hectare with the soil amendment that served it best, against about €2,300 for the sensitive, high-yielding variety grown as usual (pp. 51–52). So the margin given up is largest on fresh land. Measured in pots, which the authors recommend repeating in the open field (p. 52). Within the year: the variety is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Margin given up is income given up, in full: a margin is what a crop leaves after its variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), and the farm's fixed costs do not fall when its storage crops take a smaller part of the rotation, the buildings, machines and paving being sunk (Polman et al., 2026, p. 17). In full may be an upper end over the long run: in Dutch farm accounts for 2014–2022, farms with a larger share of ware and seed potatoes, onions and winter carrots carry significantly higher non-allocated costs per hectare (Polman et al., 2026, p. 15), but changes within a farm over the years explain little of these costs, the explained variation lying between farms, and the estimate, by the authors' account biased and less reliable, is available only from the authors on request (pp. 5, 12–13). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: Higher prices for the current crops raise the income from them: a farm's income is its revenue minus the costs it pays and depreciation (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), and Dutch arable farms' income fell to an estimated 60,000 euro per unpaid labour unit in 2025 on lower prices, after favourable growing conditions and higher yields in north-west Europe and beyond, slightly rising costs adding to the fall (van der Meulen, 2025). How far a farm's income follows the price depends on how it sells (World prices of conventional crops). Measured nationally. Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile, and those who can pay for it store more.
attributes.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of storing water, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Freshwater storage measures itself, whose description says how farmers weigh storing against their other ways through a dry summer. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to store, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

attributes.description: What a storage measure costs comes out of the money left to invest: its investment in the year it is built, and its upkeep and energy each year it runs. For the island's farms, from a drainage firm's quotes at 2021 prices, anti-salinisation drainage costs about €2,500 a hectare over a life of 15 years, and double drainage €6,000 a hectare to collect the water, with €12,500 to €25,000 for a pump to a basin and €1.80 to €4.00 per m³ for the basin (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 33–34); the creek-ridge infiltration system designed for a cluster of farms on the island's eastern creek ridges, €140,000 to €200,000, written off over about 15 years (p. 50). A year's running costs, figures the study takes from earlier studies, start at €50 for a weir (p. 19), while a creek-ridge infiltration system takes €1,440 in electricity alone (p. 20). The study finds the investment costs high, and for many farms too risky to bear alone (pp. 4–5). Within the year it is built.

attributes.description: The more of the current crops' harvest salt takes, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against them, so the more farmers grow it, but only past a threshold: Dutch farmers in salinised areas mostly hold back from saline agriculture unless salt severely hits their production (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 57). In interviews across the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them, salt in a field was largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield hard to put down to salt alone, and the damage not yet significant enough to make it urgent; it would take more dry summers like 2018 (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216). Nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, for lack of markets, the soils' intolerance of salt and the hand work they take (p. 221). In Zeeland most farmers still grow the common salt-sensitive crops (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), and on the island the response a source shows is giving up a sensitive crop, sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31), not taking up a new one. The shift the island's farmers do show is to a crop they already grow, from onions to cereals, which the source puts down to drought (Raat et al., 2026, p. 49); the island grows proportionally fewer potatoes and vegetables, mainly onions, and more cereals, which tolerate salt better, than Goeree-Overflakkee, which is connected to the main water system and so can take in fresh water (p. 34, which names no data source or year). Many of the interviewees across the provinces see research on the salt tolerance of cash crops, especially of cultivars already on the market, as contributing to resilience to salt (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 221). Years, as farmers come to see the damage over dry summers: a delay.
attributes.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of new salt-tolerant crops, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a new crop against their current crops. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description. Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what salt takes.

attributes.description: Assured offtake lowers the risk of a new crop, so more farmers grow it.
attributes.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of new salt-tolerant crops, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a new crop against their current crops. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

attributes.description: A better price after transport makes a new crop more worthwhile against the current crops, so more farmers grow it. In France, the prices of pulses are reported not high enough against major crops such as wheat, so more price incentives are needed for farmers to grow them, and most stakeholders want outlets of higher value (Magrini et al., 2018, p. 9); a specific incentive to farmers in 2010 doubled the area of pulses in its first year, and it fell back the next, downstream actors not particularly interested in them (Meynard et al., 2018, p. 10); in the Netherlands' salinising provinces, Zeeland among them, nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, mostly for lack of markets, the soils' intolerance and the hand work they take (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 221). In the Netherlands, interviews on quinoa and seed potatoes on saline soil found the lack of economic benefits the main constraint on scaling them (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 276). The same interviews, conducted as a contribution to the EU's North Sea Region SalFar project, find Dutch quinoa grown under contract for one distributor, which buys a pre-agreed amount at a fixed price and manages supply according to demand, a dependency interviewees name as hampering its uptake (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 266, 268, 277). Where a crop is sold this way and no other buyer competes, as none had for quinoa (p. 268), that means a better price raises the hectares only as far as the buyer contracts more. Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Growing a new crop, on their own fields or their neighbours', teaches farmers how.

What a switch costs comes out of the money left to invest, in the year a field changes crop. Switching tends to be costly, its investments weighed against the chance that the new crop pays more than the current one, a horticulture trade site writes (HortiDaily, 2014), and for Dutch arable farms the investments or the time needed to change their operations, among other things, leave little room to take on climate and biodiversity (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4). What a switch costs depends on the crop: quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine (van Loo, 2023, p. 75). No source read gives what a switch costs on the island. Within the year.

attributes.description: More hectares of new crops on the island, more harvest to process. Quinoa yields about 2,000 kg a hectare on average in Europe (van Loo, 2023, p. 79), and its yield varies from under 500 to over 4,000 kg (p. 76), harvested in August of the year it is sown (p. 75): within the year.

Within the year: a season's harvest.

attributes.description: More harvest within reach makes a plant or chain nearby more worthwhile, so buyers and processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than handle the crops elsewhere. In France, the firms that store, process and sell crops specialised in a few dominant ones for economies of scale, and their logistics are not adapted to sorting pulses out of mixed crops (Magrini et al., 2018, pp. 3, 9), and a small volume spread out or far from its users costs more to collect and to source (Meynard et al., 2018, pp. 7–8): the economies of scale hold wherever a chain is built, so the mechanism transfers. In the Netherlands, on Terschelling's saline field, producers of processed products are more concerned about volumes than the restaurants are, and stakeholders describe a chicken and egg: a producer needs a market, and a reliable market needs ample supply (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 14); for quinoa, one expert says efforts only work with concentrated investments and high volumes (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 270). Years: a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a): a delay.

attributes.description: A plant or chain nearby takes the harvest at less cost to move and store it, so more of the price reaches the farmer. In France, minor crops grown far from their processor cost much to collect for their volume, one cooperative building a linseed chain paid farmers a premium to deliver to its silo, and those without storage suited to small batches sold them fast, below the best price (Meynard et al., 2018, p. 7): the cost of moving and storing a harvest rises with distance and falls with volume wherever a chain runs, so the mechanism transfers. No source read gives what farmers on the island are paid. A plant that is large against the harvest within its reach can still pay less than the crop is worth to it: in Indiana, USA, where corn farmers pay the transport to the plant, a model estimates that transport cost, by softening competition from rival buyers, let plants pay on average 0.49 dollars a bushel (9% of the corn price) below the corn's value to them net of processing cost, and capacity running full added 0.18 dollars (Jung et al., 2022, pp. 614–616). Within the year: the price is set each season or contract.

attributes.description: Plants off the island are where the island's growers can sell a new crop now, at the plant's price less the haul: most Dutch quinoa growers have contracts with GreenFood50 (DutchNews.nl, 2026), based in Wageningen, which has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities, to cut transport (GreenFood50, n.d.). That more processing elsewhere raises that price, by processors competing for the harvest or by a plant nearer the island, no source read shows. Within the year: the price is set each season or contract.

attributes.description: Growing the current crops year after year builds up know-how in growing, storing and selling them, and that know-how is of little use for a new crop.
attributes.simplification: Folds Know-how of the current crops, a stock between the two: growing the current crops builds know-how, which is of little use for a new crop. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +), so no loop through the link changes, and know-how is no actor's decision. What one link leaves out: the know-how as a stock of its own, built up over years of growing the crops.

attributes.description: The more a farm owns that only its current crops can use, the more a switch leaves idle: a store still stands when its crops take a smaller part of the rotation, and its costs do not fall (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), and expensive machines are in some cases suited to one or a few crops (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). What a new crop can use is not lost (Capital lost on switching). A machine or building can still earn after its crop leaves the farm when it is rented out or used for work for other farms: nationally, a relatively large share of arable farms with a standard output below 250,000 euro have other income, such as from renting out machines or buildings or from contract work (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 36). The source does not say whether that work uses root-crop machines or stores, and a salinity shock that moves the island's farms off the same crops at once may shrink that work too, which no source read measures. Within the year, at the moment of switching.

attributes.description: What a farm's capital would stop earning holds it to its current crops. Of four arable farmers interviewed about a scheme for less intensive rotations, one, in the loess of Limburg, had recently built a store, which stands and which they want to use, and they and a farmer with plans for water storage said the investment has to be used, so that the onions stored, for example, would not soon leave the rotation (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 57, 71). Investments in expensive machines suited to one or a few crops keep a contractor and a farmer dependent on those crops for a long time (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). It holds while the crops can be grown: in the island's low polders, where the surface water is salty all year, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). On the island as a whole the lack of fresh water seems to set the share: its one interviewed farmer, with half his rotation in root crops, judged the calculated move to a less intensive rotation relatively cheap to reach there "door zoetwatergebrek" (for lack of fresh water), and the workshop held high-margin crops no option on an island with little fresh water (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57, 59). An exploration of the island by the water institute KWR sees a clear shift to less intensive crops in response to drought, fewer onions and more cereals, and relatively fewer potatoes and vegetables, mainly onions, than on Goeree-Overflakkee, which can take in fresh water from the main water system (Raat et al., 2026, pp. 34, 49). Within the year, as the rotation is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Money left to invest can go to carrying on: wells, irrigation, drains, a new harvester.

The more of the rotation is potatoes and onions, the more a farm spends on what they need: in farm accounts across the Netherlands from 2014 to 2022 a larger share of ware potatoes, seed potatoes, onions and winter carrots goes with significantly higher costs that no crop is charged with, buildings and machines among them, and storing these crops takes a store (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 5, 11, 15). The authors estimate the crops' effect with a random-effects model whose assumption they call very strong and probably untrue: they limit the bias with control variables, but call the results less reliable (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 5, 12–13). In France, specialising in a few crops is explained in part by writing off the equipment (Magrini et al., 2018, p. 3). The differences lie mostly between farms, less in how one farm changes over the years (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4): machines are written off at 8.2% a year and buildings at 3%, about 12 and 33 years if written off evenly (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 13). Years, so a delay.

attributes.description: Spending adds to this capital as far as it buys machines and stores for the current crops, not wells or drains: on Dutch arable farms the main category of investment is machines, implements and installations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19, from national farm accounts), and a store for long keeping is a mostly insulated building with a cooling installation (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 5).

attributes.description: A farm pumps groundwater only through a well it has paid for: in Zeeland extraction is allowed only with horizontal wells, from fresh water more than 15 m thick, outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26); on the island's eastern creek ridges some farmers have laid a deep drain to take water from the ridge (p. 38) and a livestock farmer irrigates from two (pp. 40, 43), and a horizontal well costs €25,000 to €40,000 (p. 49). Within the year, once the well is in.
attributes.simplification: Stands for the whole effect on pumping of a farm's dependence on its current crops, the direct link from Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops folded into this chain: the high-value crops' need for water in a dry spell is in words here. The sign is the chain's (+, then +), so no loop changes its polarity. What it leaves out: a farm that already has wells can irrigate more of a thirsty crop within the year, while the chain runs through the delay on Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops → Spending on keeping the current crops.

attributes.description: A farm with less equity against its debt is a riskier loan: a high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19), and more financing still requires a contribution of the farm's own (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3). Dutch banks assess investment plans by cash flows, solvency rates and the entrepreneur's track record (van der Meulen & van Asseldonk, 2017, p. 2), and a Rabobank adviser holds that a farm may be expected to have a solvency of at least 30 or 40% (Banken.nl, 2019). Banks weigh it beside the farm's cash flow, which counts more and more (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). In a simulation of banks' check on 264 Dutch dairy farms, 2009–2017, with two criteria the author set (a new loan within the repayment capacity from past net cash flow, and solvency not below 30%), solvency was the limit for only 1.2% of farm observations, and the author holds that solvency rarely limits a bank loan because most Dutch dairy farms are rich in land, which gives banks the confidence that they will recover their finance even in default (Lamkowsky, 2023, pp. 51, 55–56, 94, 101). Dutch arable farms had on average a higher solvency still, 81% in 2018 against 74% on dairy farms, though it differs widely within each type (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 21), and the study calls its test conservative, as Dutch banks might have lent more thanks to dairy farms' high solvency (Lamkowsky, 2023, p. 60). Within the year: a bank judges it with each loan.

attributes.description: A public plan that may change what a farm can earn enters its bank's assessment before the plan is decided. After the government announced its nitrogen plans in June 2022 (Rabobank, 2025, p. 246), a significant part of Rabobank's loans to livestock farmers migrated to stage 2, where the bank places the exposures it considers to have a significant increase in credit risk, which it called also a reflection of the high level of uncertainty (Rabobank, 2023, p. 62); in 2024 it still held an adjustment of 23 million euro to its expected credit losses for the uncertainty the plans left, scoring livestock farmers on the profitability and sustainability of their business model (Rabobank, 2025, p. 246), and its lending criteria include a farm's nearness to a Natura 2000 area (p. 83). Measured for the nitrogen plans and livestock farms across the Netherlands; no source read shows a bank weighing a water level plan, and the mechanism transfers by the bank's test, whether the farm will keep earning enough to meet its obligations, which it applies to every farm loan (Farm income → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans). Within the year: the bank updates its vulnerable sectors at least every half-year (Rabobank, 2023, p. 62).

attributes.description: Banks lend less to farms they see as riskier: they have become more critical in lending, counting farm loans riskier despite the land as security (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47), and hold back on investments not yet proven to pay (p. 8); Dutch farms' bank loans have fallen slightly in recent years, partly through the stricter rules (p. 19). Rabobank, which finances about 85% of Dutch farmers, says that since 2012, in a riskier world, it has often limited the level of financing on farms, and that a farm should be able to bridge two bad years without the bank (Banken.nl, 2019). Rabobank's outstanding agricultural loans fell by 4.3 billion euro between 2010 and 2018, to 26 billion euro, but largely because farmers asked for less credit amid uncertainty over future environmental and climate rules, the bank's stricter stance a further cause, so the fall does not measure this link alone (Banken.nl, 2019, the financial daily FD's calculation from Rabobank's annual reports, for the Netherlands as a whole and all farm types, on a news site that lists Rabobank as a partner). What the bank charges for the risk is Risk premium on farm loans. Within the year: a bank decides on a loan when it is asked.

attributes.description: Banks charge more for loans they see as riskier: the expected losses and the capital held against a loan, which the premium covers, rise with the credit risk the bank sees in the farm's creditworthiness, the size of the loan, its security and the sector's prospects (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), and within the terms agreed a bank can change the premium during the loan when the farm's creditworthiness changes (n.d.-b). Where a bank judges a farm investment too risky it may also refuse the loan outright: 51% of the surveyed Dutch farms whose loan application was rejected (15% of medium- and long-term applications in 2017) named too high an investment risk as a reason, though banks put their rejection rate for farmers at 1–2%, and stakeholders interviewed say banks are more inclined to reject loan applications based on untested innovative ways of farming (fi-compass, 2020, pp. 17, 24, 33, a study made with EU funding, measured in a survey of 301 Dutch farms, not split by sector, on their 2017 applications). Within the year: the bank sets the premium with each loan and can revise it during the loan.

attributes.description: Credit is part of what a farm can invest: banks steering their lending more by cash flow can leave less room to invest in developing the farm and in sustainability (van der Meulen et al., 2020, pp. 47–48), and a farm short of cash, once savings and cuts fall short, can ask its bank to defer part of its interest and repayments or for more credit (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28). The link has force mainly where a farm's own funds fall short: in an unbalanced panel of 264 Dutch dairy farms (accounts 2006–2017, measured on dairy, not arable, farms), the share that the model classified as financially constrained compared with their peers fell from 44% in 2009 to 8% in 2017, and a simulated stricter Basel IV lending scenario would have raised the share over the whole period only slightly, from 28.1% to 31.0% (Lamkowsky, 2023, pp. 44, 55, 57–58). Dutch farms in the fi-compass survey that did not apply for a loan in 2017 gave as main reason sufficient own funds (54.6%) or an earlier loan that already covered their needs (48.8%) (fi-compass, 2020, p. 22, the whole agriculture sector, not arable farms alone), while interviewed stakeholders place the hard access to bank finance with young farmers and new entrants, and the study adds farmers with untested ideas that banks see as too risky (p. 9). Within the year: credit granted is capacity at once.

attributes.description: A new loan adds to a farm's debt while its equity stays the same, so its debt rises relative to its assets and its solvency falls, solvency being its equity as a percentage of its total capital minus deferred tax (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Refinancing replaces a loan and adds no debt: the link counts the new money. Farms that expanded in recent years have a lower solvency (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); Dutch farmers under 45 had 68% in 2018 against 76% for those over 65, their higher long-term debt going partly with taking over the farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26); on dairy farms heavy investment and poor results together took five points off solvency between 2006 and 2015 (Silvis et al., 2017, p. 2). The sign holds with the assets' value unchanged: the debt of Dutch arable farms rose 38% between 2010 and 2022, yet in 2022 it was 28% of their balance sheet, the smallest share in farming, as equity grows mainly through the rising value of the land (CBS, 2024). Less credit slows the debt's rise; the debt itself falls through repayments. Within the year: a loan is on the balance sheet once it is paid out.

attributes.description: More credit, more to pay each year: a farm's financing charges are the interest and commission on its loans and the repayment, the periodic amount that pays a loan back within the agreed term (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), so each new loan adds its interest and repayment to what the farm pays. Within the year, from the loan's payout.

attributes.description: A higher premium raises the interest farms pay: a loan's rate changes when its specific premium does (ABN AMRO, n.d.-b), and the farms' operations often leave little or no room for higher financing costs (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). The bank sets the premium with each new loan and may revise it during a loan within its terms (ABN AMRO, n.d.-b), so the change reaches the payments as loans are made or revised: within the year, the source giving no timing. The banks' sector body's code of conduct bars a bank from changing a fixed rate during its fixed-rate period, or a premium agreed as fixed for a period, unless the client breaches its loan terms, while a variable premium may change, for example with a change in the client's risk profile (Nederlandse Vereniging van Banken, 2023, p. 15), so on a loan under the code with a fixed total rate or a fixed premium a higher premium reaches the payments only at the next reset, a new loan or a breach. These rules hold for loans requested from 1 July 2023, earlier loans from 1 July 2018 falling under the code's first version (p. 9), and for clients with a yearly group turnover up to 5 million euro and loans totalling up to 2 million euro (p. 5), a loan limit the average Dutch arable farm's bank loans of almost 1 million euro in 2018 stay within (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 21); no source read gives the island's farms' debt. No source read gives how much of the farms' debt carries a premium the bank can revise.

attributes.description: Interest is a cost that lowers a farm's income. Income is revenue less the costs paid and depreciation, plus extraordinary items (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), a definition that does not name repayments, yet the arable farms with a positive net cash flow, 55% in 2016, received enough to meet their payment obligations, repayments included, and 3% had a cash flow so low that they may not survive (p. 23): the link joins the two as one assumption, so that repayments reach what a farm can invest through its income, which keeps every loop's polarity.

attributes.description: A farm with high debt payments keeps its lucrative but salt-sensitive crops to meet them. No source read tests this, so its sign is the hypothesis's question: a farm with more debt may instead choose less risky crops.

With more bank credit more farmland is bought, and with less, less: the land a farm can acquire depends on its income and expected income together with its financing (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2); with arable returns swinging, banks want larger buffers, which leave less room to finance land, and with a land loan calculated over at most 30 years with repayment, financing land has grown ever harder, which loosens the tie between owning land and using it, while younger farmers, by Rabobank's account, care less about expanding by purchase and are open to lease (pp. 3–4). The route the other way, a farm refused credit selling up, no source read shows: few Dutch farms go bankrupt, 45 in 2016, a large part of farm bankruptcies being in greenhouse horticulture, and a farm short of cash first saves on its spending or uses its savings, and only where that is not enough can ask its bank to defer part of its interest and repayments or for more credit, the bank weighing its continuity over the long term (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28). Measured nationally. Within the year: a purchase follows its financing.

attributes.description: A farm without a successor is more likely to end when its farmer stops, its land then coming onto the market: over the long term the number of Dutch farms falls by 2 to 3% a year, mainly as farms end at the change of generation, the lack of a successor among the reasons, and the farmers who downsize or end their farm mainly set the supply of land (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2). Measured nationally. The land changes hands as the farm ends.

attributes.description: Owners attached to their land keep it rather than sell it. In the Krimpenerwaard, the wish not to lose their land, from an emotional bond with it, was an important reason owners chose to turn it into nature themselves rather than sell it, and for one farm its bond with the land weighed more than moving (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 11, 49, 68). Measured where a plan for nature, with expropriation as its last step, left owners only those choices; no source read measures it on the island's land market. Within the year: it acts when an owner decides whether to sell.

attributes.description: Expropriated land passes to the body that expropriates it when a notary's deed of expropriation is entered in the public registers (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.18), which can be drawn up only once the expropriation order and the plan it carries out are irrevocable and the provisional compensation is paid (art. 11.16); on the island, the order for the high-voltage station takes effect only once the court has confirmed it (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026, p. 1). Years, so a delay: in the Krimpenerwaard, under the law before the Omgevingswet, the order of October 2020 left two years before the owners still without an agreement had to be summoned to court, by October 2022 (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 26, 45), and the process of the owners expropriated by the court ran more than 61 months on average (p. 67), with continued use of the land until it was handed over (p. 41).

attributes.description: Land that changes hands leaves arable farming when its next holder does not farm it.

Where arable farming still pays, its holder, present or next, keeps the land arable, while what arable farming earns, not what other uses would bid, sets the land's price. A decade or more: land leaves arable use only when a holder gives it up, and just over 1.5% of Zeeland's farmland is sold in a year (Agricultural land value).

Arable land needs lower ditch levels than grassland or nature. By the water board's rules for its whole area, a water level plan starts from an optimal level for each use and soil, the farmland's derived from the optimal drain depths for farming: for arable farming and horticulture 120 cm below the surface on salt-marsh clay (schorgronden) with no sand within 1.2 m, down to 60 on peat, for permanent grassland as a rule 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 7, 19), and for nature 0 cm as a general starting point, its levels set with the site managers, as Duiveland's analysis applied them to its land-use map of 2018 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 16–17, 29). So the more hectares farmed as arable land, the more land whose farmers need low levels, in spring as their soil work allows (2021a, p. 66); how strongly they ask for them, no source read shows (Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). Within the year: the need goes with the land's use each season, while the land leaves arable use only as it changes hands (Arable land in the polders).

attributes.description: A farm that pays finds a successor more easily.

A draft plan that would leave a field with less drainage depth than its use needs gives its owner reason to expect the land to earn less and so be worth less, before any level changes, and owners concerned that a plan lowers their land's value object to it and ask to be compensated; what the level itself does once it takes effect runs, years later, through Polder drainage depth and Spring workability of the fields to Agricultural land value. Respondents to Friesland's peat meadow programme said the uncertainty it creates for a farm's future value lowers the value of land and buildings before the programme takes effect, the 'planological shadow' (Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, pp. 3, 31). In their views on draft level plans owners named that fall: in two peat polders, holding the water board liable or asking for a compensation scheme (Graas, 2021, pp. 5, 24), and calling a plan unacceptable because its burden fell on the farmers, in the value of their land and buildings among others (Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, pp. 5, 16–17), and in the Tielerwaard, on a raise beside a Natura 2000 area, the whole farm's as already at issue once the buffer zone was set (Waterschap Rivierenland, 2019, zienswijze 09). A water board compensates only damage beyond the normal societal risk, the rest staying, wholly or partly, with the owner (Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, p. 16; Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 14). Whether and how far land loses value the minister called unclear for the peat meadow areas, the question being whether the yield can stay the same or the farmer can earn a comparable income on the land another way (Minister van Landbouw, Natuur en Voedselkwaliteit, 2021, pp. 2–3). Measured elsewhere, in polders where the level change answers subsidence; it transfers as an owner's response to a plan that would leave a field too wet for its use, as in the Braakman near Terneuzen in 2015, where the island's own water board answered ZLTO, objecting for seven farmers, that some would be left with less than optimal drainage depth or with drains under water in winter, both naming damage, not the land's value (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). On the island the raises of 2021 were to limit drought damage and give the crops more moisture (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 69; 2021b, p. 53): no view on either plan, as the board summarises them, gave the land's value as a reason, the only ones against a raise naming flooding in extreme rain (2021a, p. 53), as farmers across the salinisation-prone provinces want their levels low against flooding and to work their fields with heavy machinery (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 217), and one submitter on each half asked about holding a higher level locally (2021a, p. 53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether a raise that leaves too little drainage depth would raise this concern on the island, no source read shows, nor objections on this ground to the other bodies' plans. In its own rule for its own plans, the island's water board says damage from a deliberate change of a field's drainage depth, as a raise is, is usually not seen as natural and is likely to have to be compensated, where possible by technical measures or by buying or exchanging land (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 15). Within the year: the views come in the six weeks a draft lies open (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17).
attributes.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so B13 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

attributes.description: Farmers who expect public bodies to keep their commitments object less. In views on draft water plans in peat areas, owners named unreliable government, a hidden agenda and agreements not kept beside their other grounds (Graas, 2021, p. 13; Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, pp. 6, 14, 85; Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, p. 29). In an experiment with students in Leiden, on a board advising the national government on carbon dioxide storage, how trustworthy the decision maker seemed explained how far they accepted the decision (Terwel, 2009, pp. 77–78, 81), and in the United States distrust of risk managers goes with political activism (Slovic, 1993, pp. 675–676). Measured elsewhere; it transfers as an owner's response to a body that plans for their land, whatever the plan's reason. That transfer gives a direction, not a strength: Terwel's participants were not personally involved in the decision making, and their own attitude to carbon dioxide storage did not change how far they accepted the advice (Terwel, 2009, pp. 80–82), whereas a farmer objecting to a plan for their own fields may judge it on their own view of it. It holds while a farmer still acts on the distrust: a view in Friesland reports 'weinig vertrouwen en veel gelatenheid' (Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, p. 7), and one submission has a small group on the island, no longer trusting the Province, starting a pipeline plan of its own (Lases, 2021, p. 2). None of the views on the island's two level plans of 2021, as the board summarises them, named trust (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53; 2021b, pp. 7–8). Within the year: the views come in the six weeks a draft lies open (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17).

attributes.description: Farmers attached to their land resist plans for it beyond what it is worth in money.

Hypothesis, with two mechanisms for the group model building session: the conflict over a plan itself may lower trust, and a plan delayed, changed or dropped after objections may teach farmers not to count on the next one. Farmers do name changing plans as a reason to distrust public bodies (Farmers' trust in government), but no source read shows a plan changed because of objections costing trust, and where a body takes up an objection those who objected may trust it more: farmers feel their input is ignored, which the Ombudsman concludes leads to distrust (Farmers' trust in government), but no source read shows input taken up raising trust, so the sign is part of the question. Within the year once a plan changes: trust can be destroyed in an instant; its recovery, slower, is in the element.
attributes.simplification: Folds Plans changed or dropped. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes. It assumes that a plan changed after objections costs trust as a plan changed for other reasons does, which no source read shows. The public bodies' decisions on their plans stay drawn, on the links from Objections to land-use plans into Water board's plans to raise ditch levels and Farmland planned for other uses.

attributes.description: Land taken against its owner's wish lowers how far farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments, the more so where they do not count the purpose as a public interest and where voluntary purchase was promised. Of 14 owners interviewed in the Krimpenerwaard, in a process of 2015–2023 with expropriation for nature as its last step, most experienced it as negative, and they often named an inequality of power; the municipal council had feared for trust between government and farming (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10, 15, 55). In interviews in the Netherlands, owners who did not count the plan as a public interest, nature development for one, were more often negative about expropriation in itself than those who did, as for roads (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, p. 180), and the chair of LTO held large-scale use against reliable government, farmers having been told that purchases would be voluntary (Neefjes, 2008, p. 3). The pressure starts before any order: the possibility of one weighs heavily on the process and on the owners' lives (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 55). No source read measures trust before and after, or on the island, where the purposes used so far are a road and the grid, those owners accept most. A tenant may gain (Adviescommissie Natuurherstel Westerschelde, n.d., p. 11). How negatively owners judge an expropriation afterwards seems to depend on its outcome and process: in the same Krimpenerwaard evaluation, paid for by the Province and municipality that ran the process and by the agriculture ministry, most of the owners interviewed were satisfied with their end situation, though half of those who sold rather than make the nature themselves were very dissatisfied, and satisfaction with the end result regularly contributed to a milder judgement of the whole process afterwards (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 9, 13, 53), and Holtslag-Broekhof et al. (2016, p. 183) conclude that expropriation need not be feared in itself where its public purpose is clearly communicated, the process is open and takes owners' interests seriously, and the owner ends in the same economic position as before. Within the year: trust can be destroyed in an instant, its recovery, slower, is in the element (Slovic, 1993, p. 677).

attributes.description: Objections delay, change or stop a plan in which the municipality designates farmland for another use, while it is pending; with none pending, they change nothing.
A plan that designates farmland for another use leads its owners and the farmers who work it to object, appeal and lobby against it.

Farmland the plan designates for another use leaves arable farming as the plan is carried out on it: the plan does not end the farming by itself. In the Krimpenerwaard, where the land-use plan designating farmland for nature became irrevocable in October 2021 (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 25), of the land of owners who settled by agreement without converting it themselves most was sold to the province, 152 hectares, or exchanged, 59 (p. 41), and 24 agreements were made for owners to turn land into nature themselves, on 171 hectares of their own and 274 leased from the province (p. 67), the largest area (p. 41), an amicable purchase or exchange being the most common outcome, closely followed by the owners' own conversion (p. 36); voluntary sale and the owners' own conversion alone had not completed it in earlier periods (p. 10). Years, so a delay: the sales took more than 30 months on average, the owners' own conversion more than 61 (p. 67). Expropriation is drawn apart (Farmland planned for other uses → Expropriation of farmland). Measured for nature in the peat meadows of South Holland; the procedure is national law, and how long it takes on the island no source read gives.

attributes.description: More winter rain soaks deep into the dunes and the sandy creek ridges, where the winter's rain surplus refills the lens (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661–3662, 3673–3675, measured on the island; van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 155, for the Netherlands). Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock.

attributes.description: A new well is judged on the fresh groundwater bodies established when it is notified (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 and its explanation), and in Zeeland pumping is allowed only from bodies of more than 15 m of fresh water (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26), so the thicker the lens, the more pumping the rules allow. The rules allow the same 800 m³ per hectare a year on any fresh groundwater body of 15 m or more, so outside the vulnerable areas a lens crossing 15 m opens pumping without a permit, under the general rules and within 8,000 m³ a year and 60 m³ an hour per extraction, but one thickening beyond it adds none (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2019, p. 18, the water board's own policy note). The map of fresh bodies is revised periodically, and wells in use that a revision leaves outside them may still be used while new ones are refused (p. 20), so a thinning lens lowers the allowance once a revision leaves it outside the fresh bodies: through new wells refused or the board forbidding an extraction that harms, or threatens to harm, the interests of groundwater management (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 lid 4 and its explanation). No delay: no source read shows how often those bodies are updated.

attributes.description: Farmers pump within what the rules allow: pumping that fails a condition is forbidden (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9, paragraph 7). Whether farms keep to it rests on their own records: the rule has them meter or time their pumping and report the volume yearly (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9, paragraph 2 c and g), and the water board wrote in 2019 that these self-reported yearly returns make it hard to check in the field whether everyone keeps to the maxima, and that, with its register of wells out of date, landowners are more likely to build wells at unsuitable locations without contacting it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2019, pp. 21–22, the board on its own enforcement). Within the year.

attributes.description: Double drainage would collect fresh drain water into a basin, from which a farm could irrigate that season, a system that works in concept but has not yet been tested in practice (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 23, 29, 32–33, for the island). What the other measures keep reaches crops through the lenses. Within the year.

attributes.description: Many farmers on the island say they want to invest in holding fresh water and hold back while how a measure works there, what it costs, risks and yields stay uncertain (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 11); they are readier to invest in a solution shown to work in practice somewhere (p. 56). What is learned can also rule a measure out where a farm's ground does not suit it: the feasibility studies in the island's low polders find the deep groundwater west of the creek ridge too saline to store fresh water in, making basins above ground the most feasible storage (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 32), and anti-salinisation drainage hydrologically feasible only with light seepage and a fairly permeable subsoil, at 2 of 5 locations (p. 33). On the test strips at Kerkwerve, on the island, the effect of anti-salinisation drainage seems limited, probably through poorly permeable unripened clay, a high ditch level and old shallow drains left largely working (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 97), though the trial's own report, Deltares and Acacia having run it (p. 73), sees indications that it would work under better conditions (pp. 97–98). How long this takes, no source read shows.

attributes.description: Where farms do not invest in measures, the techniques are not refined or adapted, nothing is learned from building them and their effects cannot be monitored, so no knowledge base forms at agricultural advisers and contractors (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 11–12). One measure built and monitored on the island taught what limited it, but left uncertain whether it freshened the rainwater lens: at the Drains2Buffer trial at Kerkwerve, built in 2013, a ditch level 10–40 cm above the deep drains' outlet limited them, while the measuring plots had freshened for a reason other than the measure, discovered only on the last measuring day (Oude Essink et al., 2018, pp. 73, 96–97, the trial researchers' own report). The farmer must also gain experience operating controlled drainage, and in a 2009 survey the systems laid in Zeeland at the end of 2008 had, partly because 2009 was dry, given no experience of storing water yet (Stuyt et al., 2012, p. 51, four farms in Zeeland, for STOWA, the regional water managers' knowledge centre). How long this takes, no source read shows.

attributes.description: Hypothesis: storing water is a long investment that a change of rules can strand, so the less farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments on water and land, the less they store. A question for the group model building session.

The board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where more than 10% of the area is too wet, 10 cm or more short of the optimum, the target level is to be lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved, and where less than 10% is, a raise is considered (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 9). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40). The test sets a criterion only for the share too wet; for the share too dry it sets none, only an aim to keep it small (2025, pp. 9–10; 2021b, p. 37), and Schouwen's study read more than 25% too dry in summer only as a sign the levels may be too low (2021b, p. 44), so a deep drainage depth need not start a raise. On Schouwen 37 of 43 sub-level areas, 85% of the area tested, were more than half too dry in winter and 31, 48% of it, in summer, the season that weighs more, while those holding 62% of it were more than 10% too wet in summer, partly because levels are held high there on purpose against peat compaction, and the board judged the level right in most of the area and proposed a raise in ten level areas, in two by more than 10 cm (2021b, pp. 37, 44–45, 53–54; the board's own report on its own plan). Years, so a delay: the test runs as a plan is prepared, which the board does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: By the water board's rules the level follows the land's use ("peil volgt functie"): the board adapts it to what an area needs (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 5), reading the use from the current land use and from the uses the municipality's land-use plan designates, with what is expected within about five years (p. 7). A plan starts from the optimal level for each use and soil, nature's set with the site managers (2021a, p. 29), and where nature and farmland share a level area on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and keeps the farm parcel draining, in one area by linking it to the neighbouring, lower area, in the other by closing a leak (2021a, pp. 60–62). So the less land is farmed as arable land, the more reason for a raise, whoever asks. By the board's own study for its plan, in most of Duiveland's level areas a raise is possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged, since levels in several are kept low on purpose to store extreme rain (2021a, p. 69), and the province's norm for that storage and discharge capacity, which the board tests against, is the same once in 25 years for arable land and grassland (2021a, pp. 12, 33–34; Provincie Zeeland, 2024, art. 3.3, p. 2), so land that goes from arable crops to grass is held to the same norm as before. In 2026 the board proposed to enlarge Duiveland's discharge capacity against flooding, and its slides give no date (2026a, slides 12, 17), though the province asks the board, as a duty of effort, to meet the norm by 1 January 2028 (Provincie Zeeland, 2024, art. 3.3, p. 2), so whether the limit lifts before 2050 is open. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: The saltier the field, the fewer of the crops most sensitive to salt a farm keeps: on low fields with strong saline seepage on the island, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Years, so a delay: salt in a field is largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield is hard to put down to it, and interviewees expected it to take more dry summers like 2018 to make salt urgent (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216, interviews in the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them).
attributes.simplification: Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what the soil shows.

attributes.description: With more fresh water a farm may keep or take on the crops that need it: on the island's low polders, with more fresh water available the farmer is open to more profitable crops, a more varied rotation, or both (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30). In Zeeland the area of sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 ha in 2024, the article naming the dry summers, the poor harvests and the lack of fresh water, four in five arable farmers having none, as farmers preferred less risky crops, while elsewhere the area grew (De Vriend, 2024b, for Zeeland). Years, so a delay: farmers respond to the seasons they have had, and the fall ran over five years of dry summers.

attributes.description: The margin given up is net of what the new crop earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), so the better a new crop pays the less a farm gives up on each hectare it moves to it. Quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small (pp. 2–3). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Banks look more and more at a farm's cash flow, whether its operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19): the bank judges whether the farmer can generate enough over the longer term for interest and repayment, the expected income being the limiting factor rather than the size of the farm (Farjon et al., 2013, section Financiering van bedrijfsuitbreiding). Basel IV steers banks further toward profitability and liquidity rather than the value of collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). So the less a farm earns, the more risk its bank sees, for owner and tenant alike; for the Netherlands. Within the year.

attributes.description: A public body can expropriate only for a use made possible in an adopted plan, a permit or a project decision (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.6), and only after a reasonable attempt to buy has failed (art. 11.7), so the more farmland planned for other uses, the more farmland within reach of an order. Only part of it comes within reach: the need to expropriate lapses where the owner shows they are willing and able to realise the planned use themselves, has concrete plans for it made known to the authority, and will realise it in the way the authority intends (art. 11.7(2)), and land the legger lists as a bergingsgebied can stay with its owner, who must tolerate flooding and the temporary storage of surface water on it (art. 10.3(4); annex, bergingsgebied). Of 481 ha inside and outside the nature boundary in the 69 files studied, 24 owners agreed to realise nature on 171 ha of their own land and 92 ha went through the court (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, measured in the Krimpenerwaard, a Zuid-Holland peat polder, in an evaluation commissioned by the Programmabureau Veenweiden Krimpenerwaard that ran it with the Province, and funded by the Province of Zuid-Holland, the municipality and the agriculture ministry). Years, so a delay: the attempt to buy and the order follow the adopted plan.
