attributes.label: R1 Salty soil takes in less rain
attributes.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium on the clay; once fresh water washes the salt out, the soil's structure collapses and recovers only over years. Less rain soaks in, less recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thins over years and saline groundwater comes closer to the roots: more salt. It runs in the low polders. The mechanism was measured after seawater floods; how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay, no source read shows. R1 may be weak on tile-drained fields such as the one measured on the island: in model computations extra winter water leaves through the intensive drainage without feeding the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, pp. 11, 12), and after a seawater flood most well-drained soils still let at least 150 mm through in winter (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157). No practice is on it: the salt it adds drives tolerant crops and varieties (B2, B1).

attributes.label: B1 Salt losses move fields to tolerant varieties
attributes.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the one grown now, so more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold. A tolerant variety loses less to salt, so the harvest lost falls. It seeks the loss at which a farmer changes variety, a hypothesis for the group model building session: unlike the move to new crops (B2), no source shows that salt losses move farmers to another variety. Tolerant varieties use the same machines, storage and know-how, so little capital is lost on them (R3). It drives tolerant varieties.

attributes.label: B2 Salt losses move fields to new crops
attributes.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against the current crops, so after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, and perhaps only past a threshold, more farmers grow it. A field moved no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take, so the harvest lost falls; the salt stays in the soil. It seeks the loss at which a farmer switches: that farmers hold back until salt severely hits their production rests on sources, what sets each farmer's threshold, through their crops, margins, buyers and bank, is a hypothesis for the group model building session. On the island no source read shows B2 at work: the shift its farmers show is from onions to cereals, a crop they already grow and no new one, which the source puts down to drought (Raat et al., 2026, p. 49). With B1 and B3 it is a way out of the same salt: switching keeps the land arable, B3 is arable farming ending. It drives new crops.

attributes.label: B3 Land leaving arable use lets levels rise and salt fall
attributes.description: More salt in the root zone takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and where arable farming no longer pays for a buyer or successor the land goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land. With less arable land the water board, whose level follows the land's use, has more reason to raise the ditch levels, over years; seepage falls, the rainwater lens thickens and the salt falls back. It seeks the salt level at which arable farming stops paying for any successor or buyer, set by crop prices, margins and the land market. With B2 and B1 it is a way out of the same salt: those keep the land arable with another crop, this one is arable farming ending, where the current crops stop paying and adapting does not pay or is not chosen. It acts only at that end: while arable farming still pays for someone, land from a farm that stops mostly goes to expanding neighbours and stays arable (Arable land in the polders), and a raise follows only where a whole level area leaves arable use, since where nature and farmland share one on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and keeps the farm parcel draining (Arable land in the polders → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). On Duiveland most raises wait for more discharge capacity, and the province's norm for storage and discharge holds for grassland as for arable land (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 12, 33–34, 69), so, by inference, a level area that goes from arable crops to grass would mostly still wait for the discharge works, and the loop is weaker still there. From salt to a raise takes decades, its slowest steps the land changing hands and the board's plan cycle.

attributes.label: B4 Deep drainage keeps fields workable
attributes.description: Where fields stay too wet to work in spring, farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, the fields drain and dry sooner, and the wish for lower levels eases. On Duiveland it has room mainly in the 10 of 31 level areas with more than 10% of their surface too wet in a normal winter, since in large parts of the area the drooglegging already exceeds its optimum by more than 40 cm (60 cm on schorgronden) (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 32, 42). It seeks fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring: what deep drainage gains a farm, R2 tracing what it costs. By keeping the current crops' spring work possible, it supports carrying on with them rather than adopting a practice.

attributes.label: R2 Debt and deep drainage feed each other through salt
attributes.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks charge a higher premium and its debt payments rise. To meet them it keeps its high-margin, salt-sensitive crops, whose spring soil work needs fields that dry early, so farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board, weighing that against raising them, plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, saline seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens thins over years, salt takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and leverage rises. It closes only through a hypothesis, Debt payments → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops, which no source read tests; where indebted farms choose less risky crops instead, the loop breaks there. It shows an unintended consequence of the deep drainage in B4: the gain comes within the season, the seepage and salt years later. It holds back new crops through the dependence it keeps up, while the salt it adds pushes towards them (B2, B1).

attributes.label: R3 Capital ties farms to their crops
attributes.description: A farm tied to its current crops spends on keeping them as machines and stores fall due, over years. The more it owns for those crops, the more a switch to a new crop would write off, and what it would lose ties it further to them. It holds back new crops, and leaves tolerant varieties of the current crops nearly untouched. On Schouwen-Duiveland R3 may be weak: its farm-level evidence is a store built in the Limburg loess and one farmer's plans for water storage, while the island's own farmer ties the low cost of a less intensive rotation there to the lack of fresh water, and the workshop and an exploration of the island tie the share of sensitive crops to it and to drought (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57, 59, 71; Raat et al., 2026, pp. 34, 49).

attributes.label: B5 Pumping relieves the shortfall
attributes.description: As the crop water shortfall grows, farmers pump more fresh groundwater, crops get more water and the shortfall shrinks, within the season. It seeks the water the crop needs, and runs only where a farm has fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick under it, on the creek ridges and dunes; the farmers talked to in the low polders do not irrigate. Across the whole island it can move little: groundwater irrigation, taken at the permitted maximum, a figure the authors call probably inaccurate, is about one hundredth of the 2018 precipitation deficit (Krajenbrink et al., 2023, pp. 44–46, 48). Where it eases the shortfall it eases the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B6), so it can hold storage back.

attributes.label: B6 Farms store water when harvests fall
attributes.description: As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile and those who can pay for it store more. Less winter rain drains away, the rainwater lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks and yields recover. It seeks the harvest at which storing stops being worth its cost, which each farmer sets against their other ways through a dry summer. On the island's two trials of the lens-growing measures the lens's growth was not clearly shown: at Kerkwerve freshening was measured at 3 of 5 locations and the effect 'lijkt daarmee beperkt' (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 97), and near Dreischor its growth was '(nog) niet aangetoond' over the measuring period, perhaps because of height differences within the plot or because the fresh-salt system responds slowly (van Hateren et al., 2025, p. 59). It drives storage, slowly, the lens taking years to respond.

attributes.label: B7 A shortfall brings calls for a supply route
attributes.description: The shorter of water the farms, the more firmly ZLTO asks for a supply route, and the deciding body weighs that call over the years a route takes to decide, pay for and build. A route would carry fresh water to the island, crops would have more to draw on and the shortfall would shrink. A route drawing on the Volkerak-Zoommeer would ease the shortfall little late in the season, when algae closed such inlets on Tholen in most years 2003–2011 (Schipper et al., 2014, p. 36); the Haringvliet source with a ring pipeline gives the best water but the highest costs (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 50). None exists, so the loop has not run yet; a study has left open who pays and who would run one. It seeks a shortfall the deciding body finds acceptable. Where it eased the shortfall it would ease the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B6).

attributes.label: B8 Pumping rules protect the lens
attributes.description: Under the creek ridges and dunes, the thicker the fresh groundwater, the more pumping the water board's rules allow. Farmers pump within that, and what they pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens. It seeks the balance between recharge and extraction on which the board set its limit. On the island the rules answer the lens at the 15 m threshold, not along it: a lens that thins while still at 15 m or more keeps the same 800 m³ per hectare (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2019, p. 18), and after a map revision leaves wells outside the fresh bodies, those in use may still be used and only new ones are refused (p. 20). It shows an unintended consequence of the pumping in B5: a thinner lens, which reaches crops only through wells, so it comes back only through what the rules allow. For storage on the creek ridges, what infiltration adds to this lens is what wells can pump.

attributes.label: R4 Storage keeps up the income that pays for it
attributes.description: A farm with more left to invest can pay for more storage measures, so less winter rain drains away, more recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks, and yield, income and what the farm can invest rise. Run backwards, a farm with little left to invest cannot pay for storage, its water gets scarcer and its income falls further: the financial pressure R2 traces through what farms do, R4 traces through what they cannot do. It runs in the low polders. It drives storage on farms with the means and holds it back on farms without.

attributes.label: R5 Storing teaches how storage works
attributes.description: The more measures are built and monitored on the island, the more its farmers, advisers and contractors know of how storage works there and what it costs, risks and yields, and the readier farmers are to invest. Run backwards, where farms do not invest nothing is learned and no knowledge base forms. It drives storage once measures are built and holds it back while few are. It reinforces where what is learned shows a measure works on the farm's ground, and not where it shows the ground unsuited: at Kerkwerve, on the island, monitoring found the effect of anti-salinisation drainage seems limited on unripened clay with a high ditch level and old shallow drains left largely working (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 97). How long this takes, no source read shows.

attributes.label: R6 Falling land value cuts the credit to switch
attributes.description: When farmland loses value, the same mortgage is more debt against the farm's assets, so banks see more risk and lend less. The farm has less to invest and moves fewer fields to new salt-tolerant crops, more of its conventional harvest stays exposed to salt, income falls and the land loses more value. It runs for farms that own their land. Dutch arable farms' solvency was generally high, 81% in 2018, owing to rising land values (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 21), against the 30% Dutch banks in general require (fi-compass, 2020, p. 26), so on many island farms a fall in land value may cut credit little. It shows an unintended consequence of the banks' response in B9: a bank limits its lending to protect itself, and farms that get less credit adapt less, which lowers the collateral further. It holds back new crops where land loses value and supports them where land keeps it.

attributes.label: B9 Banks lend less as leverage rises
attributes.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks lend it less, less new debt is added and its leverage stops rising. It seeks the leverage a bank accepts, and is the banks' intended loop: they limit their exposure. By limiting credit it holds back what a farm can invest in new crops and storage; R6 shows what that can do in turn.

attributes.label: B10 Switching gives up margin
attributes.description: Moving a field to a new salt-tolerant crop gives up the current crop's margin, most on fresh land where the current crops still do well. Income and land value fall, leverage and the bank's risk rise, credit falls and the farm has less to invest, so fewer fields move. It seeks the share of new crops that a farm's income and credit can carry. It shares its chain with R6, where the switch saves harvest instead; a sign cannot say which pulls harder, so that is a question for the group. It holds back new crops.

attributes.label: R7 Growers draw a plant, and a plant draws growers
attributes.description: More hectares under new salt-tolerant crops give more harvest within reach of a plant, which makes a local plant more worthwhile to buyers and processors. A plant nearby cuts transport, farmers keep more of the price, the crop is worth more and more farmers grow it. Run backwards, few hectares leave no reason for a plant and transport keeps the price low. It drives new crops once enough is grown and holds them back while too little is. Where a new crop is sold under contract to one buyer, as Dutch quinoa is in interviews published in 2022, that buyer purchases a pre-agreed amount and no other buyer competes (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 266, 268), which means a nearby plant draws more growers only as fast as the demand that buyer supplies grows.

attributes.label: B11 The water board raises levels against seepage
attributes.description: Lower ditch levels raise the saline seepage. The water board names the salinisation a concern and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses, so over years more seepage gives it more reason to plan raises; once carried out, the levels rise and the seepage falls. It seeks the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep; how far seepage weighs against drought in its plans, no source read shows. On the island the board's accounts read give the loop little support: the board raises levels on Schouwen to limit drought damage, with larger fresh water stocks in the soil as the effect (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 53), and its 2025 framework for level plans names neither seepage nor the lenses among its criteria (2025, pp. 9, 12), so of the accounts read only the Duiveland report names the lenses among its reasons for a raise (2021a, p. 37). It touches adoption only through the salt it lowers (B2, B1).

attributes.label: B12 The board tests the drainage depth
attributes.description: The water board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where little of the area is too wet a raise is considered, where much of it is the target level is lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved. Carried out over years, the depth moves back towards that optimum, which the board sets by its own rules. It touches adoption only through the seepage and salt the depth sets.

attributes.label: B13 Objections hold back plans
attributes.description: A plan to raise ditch levels brings objections, appeals and lobbying from landowning farmers who expect it to lower their land's value; whether that is their reason is a question for the group model building session. Objections can delay, change or stop the plan while it is pending, so fewer raises stay planned. On the island the views changed neither 2021 level plan, as the board summarises them, not Schouwen's raise in ten level areas nor Duiveland's proposed study of a raise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 8, 53; 2021a, p. 53), so no source read shows objections holding back a raise there. It is the objectors' intended loop, protecting their land, and seeks a plan they can accept. It touches adoption only through the levels it holds, and through R8 and R9.

attributes.label: R8 Falling land value brings objections that keep salt high
attributes.description: When farmland loses value, its owners may object harder to the next plan to raise ditch levels; whether they do is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the sign possibly opposite where compensation pays more than the land would fetch. Objections can hold today's level while a plan is pending, and never deepen it. Seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens stays thin, salt takes more of the harvest, income falls and the land loses more value. It shows an unintended consequence of the objections in B13: owners object to protect their land, and the levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower its value. It touches adoption through the salt it keeps up (B2, B1).

attributes.label: R9 Changed plans erode trust
attributes.description: Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans after public bodies have announced them. Plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one, their trust in government falls, and farmers who trust less object more. The step from objections to trust is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the step from trust back to objections rests on sources. It reinforces where farmers' objections are passed over, or through the conflict itself; where a body takes them up, the step may turn positive and the loop balancing. It holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand, as trust falls.

attributes.label: B14 Expropriation makes the next plan harder
attributes.description: The more farmland the municipality plans for other uses, the more lies within reach of an expropriation order, after the attempt to buy has failed, over years. Expropriation lowers farmers' trust in government, farmers who trust less object more, and objections delay, change or stop the next plan, so less farmland is planned. It shows an unintended consequence of expropriating for a plan: the next plan becomes harder to adopt. It seeks the planned area the island's farmers will accept. The steps through trust rest on sources; that objections lower the farmland planned is a hypothesis for the group model building session. On the island the orders sought so far are for a road and the grid, not nature (Besluit rotonde N59, 2020, p. 3; Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026, p. 1); road infrastructure is the study's example of a use designated a public interest, nature development its example of a plan some owners disputed served one, and owners who disputed it were more often negative about expropriation (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, p. 180), a study that does not cover the grid, and in the Krimpenerwaard owners' satisfaction with their end result regularly contributed to a milder judgment of the whole process afterwards (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 13), so the step through trust may be weak there; no source read measures it on the island. Through the trust it lowers it holds back storage.

maps.name: 01 CLD model
02 Actor Map
maps.description: The level at which an actor works, from global at the top to local at the bottom. Within a band, an actor's position says nothing about its scale or influence: it is placed only so that its relations are easy to follow.

maps.name: 03 C1 Salt builds, and farms respond in steps
maps.description: Salt in the root zone damages the soil's structure, less rain soaks in, the rainwater lens thins and more salt reaches the roots, in the low polders (R1). The responses differ in speed and cost: a tolerant variety uses the same machines and needs little capital (B1), a new crop comes after a delay (B2), and over years land leaves arable use (B3). The first two lower what salt takes from the harvest and leave the salt in the soil, so they ease the pressure that leads to the third, the one that lowers the salt, through the higher ditch levels that follow. The order is a reading of the delays and the costs, a hypothesis for the group model building session.

maps.name: 04 C2 Low ditch levels: workable fields now, more demand later
maps.description: Low ditch levels dry the fields sooner, within the season, and the farmers' demand for low levels eases (B4). The same low levels raise saline seepage, the rainwater lens thins over years, salt takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, debt payments rise and the farm depends more on its high-margin crops, whose spring work needs low levels, so the demand comes back higher (R2). The relief comes first and the extra demand years later, on the same variable. R2 comes back through debt and dependence, not through a wetter field, and the link from debt payments to dependence is a hypothesis for the group model building session.

maps.name: 05 C3 Debt and capital together keep a farm in its crops
maps.description: Debt payments raise a farm's dependence on its high-margin crops (R2), and so does what it would write off on machines and stores if it switched (R3); the link from debt payments is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the one from what a switch would write off rests on sources. Each loop raises the variable that drives the other: more dependence brings more spending on machines and stores for those crops and more demand for low ditch levels, so the two add up. Dependence holds back new crops, so a farm can stay with its current crops while salt, on its own, lowers that dependence over the years.

maps.name: 06 C4 The quick answer to a dry summer goes first
maps.description: Three loops answer one crop water shortfall at three speeds: pumping within the season (B5), storage over the years the rainwater lens takes to thicken (B6), and a supply route after the years it takes to decide, pay for and build, which has not run yet (B7). Whatever eases the shortfall first lowers the pressure for the slower answers. Pumping is tied to what it draws on: under the creek ridges and dunes, the thinner the lens, the less the water board's rules allow (B8). The quick answer and the slow one are largely on different farms: pumping where a thick lens lies under the farm, storage through the rainwater lens in the low polders, where the farmers talked to do not irrigate.

maps.name: 07 C5 Storing: more worthwhile, harder to pay for
maps.description: R4 and B6 share the chain from storage measures through the rainwater lens and the shortfall to the harvest, and part ways there. A worse harvest makes storing more worthwhile to a farmer (B6), and leaves the farm less income and less to invest (R4), so the same harvest pushes storage up and down. Farms with the means store and farms without may not, though they face the same water. Which pull is stronger differs per farm: a sign cannot show it, and the group model building session can test it, both links into storage being hypotheses. It runs in the low polders.

maps.name: 08 C6 Salt losses raise the wish to switch and cut the means
maps.description: The harvest lost to salt makes a new salt-tolerant crop worth more against the current crops, after a delay (B2). The same losses lower income and land value, so a bank sees more risk and lends less and the farm has less to invest in the switch (R6); limiting credit is how the bank keeps its own exposure down (B9). A field that moves saves harvest from salt (R6) and gives up the current crop's margin (B10), most on fresh land, so the salt on the field decides whether the switch adds income or costs it. Which of these is stronger, a sign cannot show.

maps.name: 09 C7 New crops stay stuck or take off
maps.description: With few hectares under a new crop there is little harvest within reach of a plant, no local plant, and transport keeps the net price low (R7), while every field moved gives up the current crop's margin, which income and credit must carry (B10), so adoption stays low. With enough hectares a plant becomes worthwhile, the net price rises and more farmers grow the crop. A higher net price also means less margin given up, by a link outside these two loops, which eases the brake B10 puts on adoption. How many hectares that takes, a sign cannot show.

maps.name: 10 C8 One ditch level between four goals
maps.description: Four balancing loops act on the water board's plans for the same ditch levels, each towards its own goal: fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring (B4), the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep (B11), the optimum the board sets for each use and soil (B12), and a plan the objecting owners can accept (B13). The goals cannot all be met at once, so the level settles where those pressures balance. How far seepage weighs against the other goals in the board's plans, no source read shows.

maps.name: 11 C9 Objections to one plan shape the next
maps.description: Objections delay, change or stop a plan, which is what owners object for (B13). Two things follow. The levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower the land's value, and a lower value may bring more objections (R8). And plans changed or dropped, and expropriation for a plan, lower farmers' trust in government, which may bring more objections to the next plan (R9, B14). Whether objections settle at a plan the owners accept or keep growing is a question for the group model building session, three of its steps being hypotheses: from land value to objections, from objections to trust, and from objections to the farmland planned. The trust it lowers also holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand.

maps.name: 12 C10 Falling land value: levels held, or land leaving arable
maps.description: The three loops share the chain from the water board's plans through the drainage depth, seepage, the rainwater lens, the salt and the harvest to income and land value, and part ways at land value. As land loses value, leverage and debt lead farmers to ask for low levels (R2) and owners may object harder to raises (R8, a hypothesis), so both keep the levels low and the salt coming. Where arable farming stops paying, land leaves arable use, the board has more reason to raise the levels, and the salt falls back (B3). The same fall sends the water board opposite signals. Which is stronger decides whether the decline runs on or stops, and a sign cannot show it.

maps.name: 13 R1 Salty soil takes in less rain
maps.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium on the clay; once fresh water washes the salt out, the soil's structure collapses and recovers only over years. Less rain soaks in, less recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thins over years and saline groundwater comes closer to the roots: more salt. It runs in the low polders. The mechanism was measured after seawater floods; how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay, no source read shows. R1 may be weak on tile-drained fields such as the one measured on the island: in model computations extra winter water leaves through the intensive drainage without feeding the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, pp. 11, 12), and after a seawater flood most well-drained soils still let at least 150 mm through in winter (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157). No practice is on it: the salt it adds drives tolerant crops and varieties (B2, B1).

maps.name: 14 B1 Salt losses move fields to tolerant varieties
maps.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the one grown now, so more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold. A tolerant variety loses less to salt, so the harvest lost falls. It seeks the loss at which a farmer changes variety, a hypothesis for the group model building session: unlike the move to new crops (B2), no source shows that salt losses move farmers to another variety. Tolerant varieties use the same machines, storage and know-how, so little capital is lost on them (R3). It drives tolerant varieties.

maps.name: 15 B2 Salt losses move fields to new crops
maps.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against the current crops, so after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, and perhaps only past a threshold, more farmers grow it. A field moved no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take, so the harvest lost falls; the salt stays in the soil. It seeks the loss at which a farmer switches: that farmers hold back until salt severely hits their production rests on sources, what sets each farmer's threshold, through their crops, margins, buyers and bank, is a hypothesis for the group model building session. On the island no source read shows B2 at work: the shift its farmers show is from onions to cereals, a crop they already grow and no new one, which the source puts down to drought (Raat et al., 2026, p. 49). With B1 and B3 it is a way out of the same salt: switching keeps the land arable, B3 is arable farming ending. It drives new crops.

maps.name: 16 B3 Land leaving arable use lets levels rise and salt fall
maps.description: More salt in the root zone takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and where arable farming no longer pays for a buyer or successor the land goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land. With less arable land the water board, whose level follows the land's use, has more reason to raise the ditch levels, over years; seepage falls, the rainwater lens thickens and the salt falls back. It seeks the salt level at which arable farming stops paying for any successor or buyer, set by crop prices, margins and the land market. With B2 and B1 it is a way out of the same salt: those keep the land arable with another crop, this one is arable farming ending, where the current crops stop paying and adapting does not pay or is not chosen. It acts only at that end: while arable farming still pays for someone, land from a farm that stops mostly goes to expanding neighbours and stays arable (Arable land in the polders), and a raise follows only where a whole level area leaves arable use, since where nature and farmland share one on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and keeps the farm parcel draining (Arable land in the polders → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). On Duiveland most raises wait for more discharge capacity, and the province's norm for storage and discharge holds for grassland as for arable land (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 12, 33–34, 69), so, by inference, a level area that goes from arable crops to grass would mostly still wait for the discharge works, and the loop is weaker still there. From salt to a raise takes decades, its slowest steps the land changing hands and the board's plan cycle.

maps.name: 17 B4 Deep drainage keeps fields workable
maps.description: Where fields stay too wet to work in spring, farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, the fields drain and dry sooner, and the wish for lower levels eases. On Duiveland it has room mainly in the 10 of 31 level areas with more than 10% of their surface too wet in a normal winter, since in large parts of the area the drooglegging already exceeds its optimum by more than 40 cm (60 cm on schorgronden) (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 32, 42). It seeks fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring: what deep drainage gains a farm, R2 tracing what it costs. By keeping the current crops' spring work possible, it supports carrying on with them rather than adopting a practice.

maps.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks charge a higher premium and its debt payments rise. To meet them it keeps its high-margin, salt-sensitive crops, whose spring soil work needs fields that dry early, so farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board, weighing that against raising them, plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, saline seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens thins over years, salt takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and leverage rises. It closes only through a hypothesis, Debt payments → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops, which no source read tests; where indebted farms choose less risky crops instead, the loop breaks there. It shows an unintended consequence of the deep drainage in B4: the gain comes within the season, the seepage and salt years later. It holds back new crops through the dependence it keeps up, while the salt it adds pushes towards them (B2, B1).

maps.description: When farmland loses value, the same mortgage is more debt against the farm's assets, so banks see more risk and lend less. The farm has less to invest and moves fewer fields to new salt-tolerant crops, more of its conventional harvest stays exposed to salt, income falls and the land loses more value. It runs for farms that own their land. Dutch arable farms' solvency was generally high, 81% in 2018, owing to rising land values (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 21), against the 30% Dutch banks in general require (fi-compass, 2020, p. 26), so on many island farms a fall in land value may cut credit little. It shows an unintended consequence of the banks' response in B9: a bank limits its lending to protect itself, and farms that get less credit adapt less, which lowers the collateral further. It holds back new crops where land loses value and supports them where land keeps it.

maps.name: 27 B9 Banks lend less as leverage rises
maps.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks lend it less, less new debt is added and its leverage stops rising. It seeks the leverage a bank accepts, and is the banks' intended loop: they limit their exposure. By limiting credit it holds back what a farm can invest in new crops and storage; R6 shows what that can do in turn.

maps.name: 28 B10 Switching gives up margin
maps.description: Moving a field to a new salt-tolerant crop gives up the current crop's margin, most on fresh land where the current crops still do well. Income and land value fall, leverage and the bank's risk rise, credit falls and the farm has less to invest, so fewer fields move. It seeks the share of new crops that a farm's income and credit can carry. It shares its chain with R6, where the switch saves harvest instead; a sign cannot say which pulls harder, so that is a question for the group. It holds back new crops.

maps.name: 29 R7 Growers draw a plant, and a plant draws growers
maps.description: More hectares under new salt-tolerant crops give more harvest within reach of a plant, which makes a local plant more worthwhile to buyers and processors. A plant nearby cuts transport, farmers keep more of the price, the crop is worth more and more farmers grow it. Run backwards, few hectares leave no reason for a plant and transport keeps the price low. It drives new crops once enough is grown and holds them back while too little is. Where a new crop is sold under contract to one buyer, as Dutch quinoa is in interviews published in 2022, that buyer purchases a pre-agreed amount and no other buyer competes (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 266, 268), which means a nearby plant draws more growers only as fast as the demand that buyer supplies grows.

maps.name: 30 B11 The water board raises levels against seepage
maps.description: Lower ditch levels raise the saline seepage. The water board names the salinisation a concern and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses, so over years more seepage gives it more reason to plan raises; once carried out, the levels rise and the seepage falls. It seeks the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep; how far seepage weighs against drought in its plans, no source read shows. On the island the board's accounts read give the loop little support: the board raises levels on Schouwen to limit drought damage, with larger fresh water stocks in the soil as the effect (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 53), and its 2025 framework for level plans names neither seepage nor the lenses among its criteria (2025, pp. 9, 12), so of the accounts read only the Duiveland report names the lenses among its reasons for a raise (2021a, p. 37). It touches adoption only through the salt it lowers (B2, B1).

maps.name: 31 B12 The board tests the drainage depth
maps.description: The water board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where little of the area is too wet a raise is considered, where much of it is the target level is lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved. Carried out over years, the depth moves back towards that optimum, which the board sets by its own rules. It touches adoption only through the seepage and salt the depth sets.

maps.name: 32 B13 Objections hold back plans
maps.description: A plan to raise ditch levels brings objections, appeals and lobbying from landowning farmers who expect it to lower their land's value; whether that is their reason is a question for the group model building session. Objections can delay, change or stop the plan while it is pending, so fewer raises stay planned. On the island the views changed neither 2021 level plan, as the board summarises them, not Schouwen's raise in ten level areas nor Duiveland's proposed study of a raise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 8, 53; 2021a, p. 53), so no source read shows objections holding back a raise there. It is the objectors' intended loop, protecting their land, and seeks a plan they can accept. It touches adoption only through the levels it holds, and through R8 and R9.

maps.name: 33 R8 Falling land value brings objections that keep salt high
maps.description: When farmland loses value, its owners may object harder to the next plan to raise ditch levels; whether they do is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the sign possibly opposite where compensation pays more than the land would fetch. Objections can hold today's level while a plan is pending, and never deepen it. Seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens stays thin, salt takes more of the harvest, income falls and the land loses more value. It shows an unintended consequence of the objections in B13: owners object to protect their land, and the levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower its value. It touches adoption through the salt it keeps up (B2, B1).

maps.name: 34 R9 Changed plans erode trust
maps.description: Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans after public bodies have announced them. Plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one, their trust in government falls, and farmers who trust less object more. The step from objections to trust is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the step from trust back to objections rests on sources. It reinforces where farmers' objections are passed over, or through the conflict itself; where a body takes them up, the step may turn positive and the loop balancing. It holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand, as trust falls.

maps.name: 35 B14 Expropriation makes the next plan harder
maps.description: The more farmland the municipality plans for other uses, the more lies within reach of an expropriation order, after the attempt to buy has failed, over years. Expropriation lowers farmers' trust in government, farmers who trust less object more, and objections delay, change or stop the next plan, so less farmland is planned. It shows an unintended consequence of expropriating for a plan: the next plan becomes harder to adopt. It seeks the planned area the island's farmers will accept. The steps through trust rest on sources; that objections lower the farmland planned is a hypothesis for the group model building session. On the island the orders sought so far are for a road and the grid, not nature (Besluit rotonde N59, 2020, p. 3; Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026, p. 1); road infrastructure is the study's example of a use designated a public interest, nature development its example of a plan some owners disputed served one, and owners who disputed it were more often negative about expropriation (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, p. 180), a study that does not cover the grid, and in the Krimpenerwaard owners' satisfaction with their end result regularly contributed to a milder judgment of the whole process afterwards (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 13), so the step through trust may be weak there; no source read measures it on the island. Through the trust it lowers it holds back storage.
